    New to this? Start here

    You should be comfortable with algebra and basic trig. The Math toolkit at the top reviews functions, exponentials and logs if you want a refresher.

    How to use a module

    1. Read The idea: the concept in everyday words.
    2. Play with the graph. Drag the points and move the sliders; the numbers underneath update as you go.
    3. Do Try this: guess first, then press Set it up for me and check.
    4. Work the Worked example one step at a time.
    5. Answer Check yourself, then do the practice problems.

    Look for dotted words: tap them for a quick definition. Every simulation has a Coach that explains whatever control you just moved, and a Reset button.

    Four ideas you'll use everywhere

    • Zoom in far enough and a curve looks like a line. That line's slope is the derivative.
    • A derivative is a rate. Always ask: rate of what, per what?
    • An integral adds up thin slices. Area, distance, volume and total change are all the same move.
    • The two are opposites. The Fundamental Theorem says so, and it is why antiderivatives work.

    Suggested path

    Following a class: go unit by unit; each module lists its AP unit.

    Before an exam: drill Which tool?, build a mixed set in Exam review, and clear your mistakes queue.

    Free response: try the original questions in FRQ practice.

    Need a number or an equation? Open the Reference button at the bottom right: derivative rules, integrals, limits and series.

    MathAB & BC

    Functions & transformations

    Before derivatives: how to read a formula as a graph. Shift, stretch and flip a parent function and see exactly what each number does.

    The idea

    Every graph in calculus is a familiar parent function that has been moved. y = a·f(b(x − h)) + k says: shift right by h, shift up by k, stretch vertically by a (flip if negative) and squeeze horizontally by b. Changes inside the parentheses act on x and act backwards (x − h moves right); changes outside act on y and do what they say.

    Functions can also be composed, f(g(x)) (do g first), and many have inverses that reflect the graph over the line y = x. Composition is what the chain rule differentiates.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    you read each graph as its own formula
    So we didn't need
    a way to see families of graphs at once
    Now
    derivatives of shifted and stretched functions come straight from the parent
    So we need
    a transformation toolkit and composition
    y = a·f(b(x − h)) + kgeneral transformation
    (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x))composition: g first
    f(f⁻¹(x)) = xinverse
    Move the parent function
    Parent

    key point moves from—
    to—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set h = 2 and k = 1 on x². Where is the vertex?

      What you should see

      At (2, 1): right 2 because of (x − 2), up 1 because of + 1.

    2. Set a = −1 on x². What happens?

      What you should see

      The parabola flips upside down: a negative a reflects the graph across the x-axis.

    3. Choose sin x and set b = 2. How does the graph change?

      What you should see

      It repeats twice as fast: the period is 2π/2 = π instead of 2π. A larger b squeezes the graph horizontally toward the y-axis, while its height stays 1.

    4. Choose |x| with a = −2 and k = 3. Where is the corner, and which way does it open?

      What you should see

      The corner moves to (0, 3), and the graph opens downward: a = −2 flips it over and also makes it steeper (slopes ±2). The equation is y = −2|x| + 3.

    5. Choose √x and set h = −2. Where does the graph start? Which way did it move?

      What you should see

      It starts at (−2, 0): the equation is √(x + 2), and + 2 inside moves the graph LEFT by 2. Inside changes act backwards, which is why x + 2 is a move to the left.

    Worked example

    If f(x) = x² + 1 and g(x) = 2x − 3, find f(g(2)) and g(f(2)).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Inside first. For f(g(2)) work out g(2) = 2·2 − 3 = 1.
    2. Then f. f(1) = 1² + 1 = 2.
    3. Now the other order. f(2) = 4 + 1 = 5, then g(5) = 10 − 3 = 7.
    4. Answer. f(g(2)) = 2 and g(f(2)) = 7. Composition is not commutative.

    Common mistakes

    • Moving the wrong way: (x + 2) shifts the graph left, not right.
    • Applying h before the stretch b when b is inside: in y = f(b(x − h)) the shift is h, not h/b.
    • Mixing up f(g(x)) and g(f(x)).
    • Treating f−1(x) as 1/f(x). It is the inverse function, not the reciprocal.

    Even, odd and inverses

    Even functions satisfy f(−x) = f(x) (mirror in the y-axis, like x²). Odd functions satisfy f(−x) = −f(x) (turn 180° about the origin, like x³ and sin x). A function has an inverse only if it passes the horizontal line test; the inverse graph is the reflection over y = x.

    Check yourself: The graph of y = (x − 3)² + 2 is the graph of y = x² moved:

    MathAB & BC

    Trig, exponentials & logs

    Sine, cosine, ex and ln x: four functions you will differentiate and integrate constantly. Here is what each one looks like and why.

    The idea

    On the unit circle, the point at angle θ (measured in radians from the positive x-axis) is (cos θ, sin θ). That one picture gives you the graphs of sine and cosine, their values at the special angles, and the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Calculus uses radians because then the arc length equals the angle.

    An exponential bx multiplies by b for every step in x. The special base e ≈ 2.718 is the one whose slope equals its height at every point. Its inverse is the natural log ln x: ln(ex) = x and eln x = x.

    Assumption upgrade

    So we didn't need

    Now

    So we need
    the unit circle in radians, and e and ln
    (cos θ, sin θ)point on the unit circle
    sin²θ + cos²θ = 1identity
    ln(ab) = ln a + ln b · ln(an) = n ln alog rules
    eln x = x · ln ex = xinverses
    The unit circle
    sin θ (blue)—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set θ = π/4 (about 0.785). What are sine and cosine?

      What you should see

      Both are √2/2 ≈ 0.707: at 45° the point sits on the diagonal, so its x and y coordinates are equal.

    2. Slide the base b to e (2.718). What is the slope of bx at x = 0?

      What you should see

      1. For other bases the slope at 0 is ln b: below 1 for b < e, above 1 for b > e. Only e makes the slope exactly equal to the height (1) at x = 0.

    3. Set θ = 3π/2 (about 4.71). What are sin θ and cos θ, and where is the point?

      What you should see

      sin θ ≈ −1 and cos θ ≈ 0: the point is at the bottom of the circle, (0, −1). The angle is measured counter-clockwise from the positive x-axis, and tan θ blows up here because cos θ = 0.

    4. Set the base b = 2, then b = 5. What is the slope of bˣ at x = 0 each time?

      What you should see

      For b = 2 the slope at 0 is ln 2 ≈ 0.693, and for b = 5 it is ln 5 ≈ 1.609. The slope of bˣ at x = 0 is always ln b, so it equals 1 only for b = e.

    Worked example

    Solve e2x = 7 for x.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Undo e with ln. Take the natural log of both sides: ln(e2x) = ln 7.
    2. Simplify. ln(e2x) = 2x, so 2x = ln 7.
    3. Solve. x = (ln 7)/2.
    4. Answer. x ≈ 0.973. Check: e1.946 ≈ 7.

    Common mistakes

    • Using degrees in calculus formulas. Set your calculator to radians.
    • Writing ln(a + b) = ln a + ln b. The rule is for products: ln(ab) = ln a + ln b.
    • Forgetting ln x is only defined for x > 0.
    • Thinking ex can be zero or negative: it is always positive.
    • Mixing up sin²θ with sin(θ²).

    The special angles

    Memorize the first-quadrant values: sin 0 = 0, sin π/6 = 1/2, sin π/4 = √2/2, sin π/3 = √3/2, sin π/2 = 1, and cosine runs the other way (1, √3/2, √2/2, 1/2, 0). The signs in the other quadrants follow from which coordinate is negative.

    AP Unit 1AB & BC

    Limits from graphs & tables

    A limit asks where a function is heading as x gets close to a number, not what the function does at that number. That one change lets calculus talk about a tangent line, a speed at an instant, and an area under a curve.

    The idea

    Walk toward a doorway along a hallway whose floor is the graph of f. As you get closer to the doorway at x = a, your height settles toward some value L. That height is the limit. It does not matter whether there is a floor tile exactly at the doorway, or whether the tile there is at a different height. The limit only cares about the approach.

    You can approach from the left or from the right. The limit exists only when both approaches head to the same height. If the floor has a step in it, the two sides disagree and the limit does not exist.

    Assumption upgrade

    limx→a f(x) = Lf(x) gets as close to L as you like
    limx→a⁻ f(x)approach from the left
    limx→a⁺ f(x)approach from the right
    left = right = Lthe limit exists and equals L

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Hole and zoom all the way in. What do both probes head toward, and what is f(a)?

      What you should see

      Both probes squeeze toward 2, so the limit is 2. But f(1) has no value (0/0): there is a hole in the graph. A limit can exist where the function has no value at all.

    2. Choose Jump and zoom in. Do the two probes ever meet?

      What you should see

      The left probe heads to 3 and the right probe heads to −1, no matter how far you zoom. Left ≠ right, so the limit does not exist. Notice f(2) = 1 is neither of them: the value at the point is irrelevant to the limit.

    3. Choose sin(1/x) and zoom in. Is there any value both probes settle toward?

      What you should see

      No. The graph keeps swinging between −1 and 1 faster and faster as x nears 0, so the probes keep jumping around. The limit does not exist, and not because of a jump: the function never settles.

    Read a limit from a graph

    Open circle = the graph does not include that point. Filled dot = the graph's value there. Tap a question to see what the graph says, then make a new graph.

    Worked example

    Estimate limx→2 (x² − 4)/(x − 2) from a table, then say why plugging in fails.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Plug in. At x = 2 the expression is 0/0, which tells us nothing. The function has no value at 2, so we look at nearby values.
    2. Left side. f(1.9) = (3.61 − 4)/(−0.1) = 3.9, f(1.99) = 3.99, f(1.999) = 3.999.
    3. Right side. f(2.1) = (4.41 − 4)/0.1 = 4.1, f(2.01) = 4.01, f(2.001) = 4.001.
    4. Compare. Both sides head toward 4, from below on the left and above on the right. So limx→2 (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = 4.
    5. Check with a graph. (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = x + 2 everywhere except x = 2, so its graph is the line y = x + 2 with a hole at (2, 4). A table gives a good estimate; the algebra in the next module will prove it.

    Common mistakes

    • Thinking the limit equals f(a). It often does (for smooth graphs), but it need not: the limit ignores the value at a.
    • Saying a limit "doesn't exist" because f(a) has no value. A hole still has a limit.
    • Reading a graph's limit from the filled dot instead of from the heights the two sides approach.
    • Believing a table proves a limit. It gives a strong estimate; oscillating functions can fool a short table.
    • Writing "lim = 3 and −1". If the two sides disagree, the two-sided limit does not exist (DNE); the one-sided limits are separate answers.

    When a limit fails to exist

    There are three common ways. A jump: the one-sided limits are both numbers but unequal. Unbounded growth: the function blows up toward ∞ or −∞ near a (the next modules call this an infinite limit; the AP exam says the limit does not exist but may describe it as ∞). Oscillation: the function keeps swinging without settling, like sin(1/x) at 0.

    The formal definition (every tolerance around L is met once x is close enough to a) is what makes this rigorous. AP Calculus works with the idea rather than the proof, but it is the reason limits can be added, multiplied and divided safely, which the next module uses.

    Check yourself: as x → 2 the graph approaches 3 from the left and −1 from the right, and f(2) = 1. What is limx→2 f(x)?

    Check yourself: the graph has an open circle at (3, 5) and approaches height 5 from both sides. Does limx→3 f(x) exist?

    AP Unit 1AB & BC

    Algebraic limits

    When plugging in gives 0/0, the function is hiding something. Algebra rewrites it into a form that does not hide it.

    The idea

    Direct substitution works whenever the function is continuous at a: just evaluate. The trouble is the form 0/0, which is not a number but a clue: the top and bottom share a factor that is going to zero. Remove the shared factor and what is left can be evaluated.

    Three moves cover almost everything. Factor and cancel (polynomials). Multiply by the conjugate (square roots). Combine fractions (a fraction inside a fraction). When a function is trapped between two others that share a limit, the squeeze theorem gives the answer.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    a limit was something you read off a table or graph
    So we didn't need
    algebra
    Now
    most limits on the exam come as formulas, not pictures
    So we need
    a way to simplify the formula until the limit is just substitution
    lim f = f(a)if f is continuous at a
    0/0factor, rationalize or combine
    g ≤ f ≤ hand lim g = lim h = L ⇒ lim f = L
    Same graph, simpler formula
    Case

    plugging in gives—
    after algebra—
    the limit—
    The algebra—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Factor. The orange dashed line is the simplified formula. Where do the two graphs differ?

      What you should see

      Only at x = 3, where the original has a hole. Everywhere else they are the same graph, so they approach the same height: the simplified formula gives the limit.

    2. Choose Squeeze. Why can't you just plug in x = 0?

      What you should see

      sin(1/0) is meaningless. But sin is always between −1 and 1, so x²·sin(1/x) is trapped between −x² and x². Both bounds go to 0, so the function is squeezed to 0.

    3. Choose Conjugate. What happens if you plug in x = 0, and what does the dashed formula give?

      What you should see

      Plugging in gives 0/0. Multiplying top and bottom by √(x + 4) + 2 leaves 1/(√(x + 4) + 2), which is 1/4 at x = 0. Check: at x = 0.1 the original is (√4.1 − 2)/0.1 ≈ 0.2485, already close to 0.25.

    4. Choose Fractions. Why is the limit negative?

      What you should see

      Combining 1/x − 1/3 = (3 − x)/(3x) gives (3 − x)/(3x(x − 3)) = −1/(3x) once the factor is cancelled. At x = 3 that is −1/9 ≈ −0.111: the numerator 3 − x is the opposite sign of the denominator x − 3.

    Worked example

    Find limx→2 (x² − x − 2)/(x − 2).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Plug in. 4 − 2 − 2 = 0 on top and 2 − 2 = 0 on the bottom: the form 0/0, so keep working.
    2. Factor the top. x² − x − 2 = (x − 2)(x + 1).
    3. Cancel the common factor. For x ≠ 2, (x − 2)(x + 1)/(x − 2) = x + 1. The limit only looks at x ≠ 2, so this is allowed.
    4. Substitute. limx→2 (x + 1) = 3.
    5. Answer. The limit is 3. The original has a hole at (2, 3).

    Common mistakes

    • Cancelling a factor that does not go to 0: only cancel the factor that is the cause of 0/0.
    • Stopping at 0/0 and writing "the limit does not exist". 0/0 means "do more work".
    • Multiplying only the top by the conjugate. Multiply top and bottom by the same thing.
    • Using the squeeze theorem with bounds that do not have the same limit.
    • Writing "= 3" after the first step. Keep "lim" until you substitute.

    Why algebra is allowed

    Two functions that agree everywhere except at a have the same limit at a, because a limit never looks at x = a itself. That is why cancelling (x − 2)/(x − 2) is legal in a limit, even though 0/0 at x = 2 is not defined.

    Check yourself: which move turns (√(x + 9) − 3)/x into something you can evaluate at 0?

    AP Unit 1AB & BC

    Continuity & the IVT

    A function is continuous if you can draw it without lifting your pencil. Calculus needs a sharper test, and one big consequence: continuous functions cannot skip values.

    The idea

    Continuity at a point means three things hold: f(a) exists, the limit as x → a exists, and they are equal. A hole, a jump or a blow-up each breaks one of the three. Continuous on an interval means continuous at every point of it.

    If a function is continuous on [a, b] it cannot skip over any value between f(a) and f(b). That is the Intermediate Value Theorem. It is why you can say a root exists in an interval without finding it.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    a graph was just a picture you could sketch
    So we didn't need
    a precise test for "no breaks"
    Now
    continuity underpins differentiation and integration theorems
    So we need
    continuity defined with limits, and the IVT
    limx→a f(x) = f(a)continuous at a
    f(c) = NIVT: some c in (a, b) for any N between f(a) and f(b)
    removable · jump · infinitetypes of discontinuity
    Make it continuous

    f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = kx − 3 for x ≥ 2. Slide k until the graph has no break.

    1. f(2) is defined—
    2. the limit exists—
    3. limit = f(2)—
    verdict—
    The Intermediate Value Theorem
    where f(x) = N—
    what this shows—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Slide k to 3. What changes in the three-part checklist?

      What you should see

      At k = 3 the right piece starts at 3·2 − 3 = 3, exactly where the left piece is heading (2 + 1 = 3). All three conditions pass: f(2) = 3, the limit is 3, and they match.

    2. Tick Break the function and set N = 2. Does any x give f(x) = 2?

      What you should see

      No. The jump skips from height 0.25 to 3.25, so heights in between are never reached. The IVT does not apply because the function is not continuous.

    3. Slide k to 1. How big is the jump?

      What you should see

      The left piece heads to 3, but at k = 1 the right piece starts at 2(1) − 3 = −1. The jump is 3 − (−1) = 4, and the verdict says discontinuous. Only k = 3 repairs it.

    4. Leave the function unbroken and set N = 3. Where does f(x) = 3, and why is it guaranteed?

      What you should see

      x² − 2 = 3 gives x = √5 ≈ 2.236. The function is continuous on [0, 3] with f(0) = −2 and f(3) = 7, and 3 is between them, so the IVT promises a solution.

    5. Tick Break the function and set N = 0. Is a crossing still found? Why does the break not matter here?

      What you should see

      Yes: x = √2 ≈ 1.414, which is left of the jump at 1.5. The break only hides the heights between 0.25 and 3.25. The IVT does not apply, but a crossing can still exist.

    Worked example

    Find k so that f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = kx + 2 for x > 1 is continuous at x = 1.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Left piece at 1. f(1) = 1² = 1, and the left limit is also 1.
    2. Right limit. As x → 1⁺ the function is kx + 2, so the right limit is k + 2.
    3. Match. Continuity needs left = right = f(1): k + 2 = 1.
    4. Solve. k = −1.

    Common mistakes

    • Checking only that the limit exists and forgetting f(a) must be defined and equal to it.
    • Calling a hole a "jump". A hole (removable) has matching sides; a jump does not.
    • Using the IVT without checking the function is continuous on the whole closed interval.
    • Thinking the IVT finds the number: it only guarantees one exists.
    • Assuming "continuous" means "differentiable". A corner is continuous but not differentiable (Unit 2).

    Types of discontinuity

    Removable: the limit exists but f(a) is missing or different. Jump: the one-sided limits are different numbers. Infinite: the function blows up (a vertical asymptote). Oscillating: the function swings forever. A removable discontinuity can be "repaired" by redefining f(a) as the limit.

    Check yourself: f is continuous on [1, 4] with f(1) = −2 and f(4) = 5. Which value must f take somewhere in [1, 4]?

    AP Unit 1AB & BC

    Infinite limits & end behavior

    What happens when the function blows up near a point, or when x gets enormous? Both questions give asymptotes.

    The idea

    A vertical asymptote at x = a means the function grows without bound as x → a: lim f(x) = ±∞ from at least one side. In a fraction it happens where the bottom is 0 but the top is not. The limit "= ∞" is shorthand: it technically does not exist, but we say how it fails.

    A horizontal asymptote comes from limits at infinity: limx→∞ f(x) = L. For a ratio of polynomials compare the leading terms: a lower-degree top gives 0, equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients, a higher-degree top gives ±∞ (no horizontal asymptote).

    Assumption upgrade

    limits were finite numbers at finite points
    So we didn't need

    Now

    So we need

    limx→a f(x) = ±∞vertical asymptote x = a
    limx→±∞ f(x) = Lhorizontal asymptote y = L
    deg top vs deg bottomcompare leading terms

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose equal degrees and zoom out. What height does the graph flatten to?

      What you should see

      Toward 2, the ratio of leading coefficients (2x² over x²). The two vertical asymptotes at x = ±1 stay put while the ends level off.

    2. Choose top higher degree and zoom out. Does it level off?

      What you should see

      No. It keeps growing, like the line y = x. A higher-degree top means no horizontal asymptote: the limit at infinity is ±∞.

    3. Choose sin x / x and zoom out. The ends go to 0. Does the graph ever touch y = 0?

      What you should see

      Yes, again and again: sin x / x = 0 at x = π, 2π, 3π, … while the waves shrink toward 0. A graph may cross its horizontal asymptote; the asymptote only describes where the far ends go.

    4. Choose top lower degree and zoom out. Which height do the ends approach?

      What you should see

      0: (3x + 1)/(x² − 4) has the higher degree on the bottom, so the bottom wins. The vertical asymptotes x = ±2 stay put.

    Worked example

    Find the asymptotes of f(x) = (3x² − 3)/(x² − 4).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Vertical. The bottom is 0 at x = ±2. The top at x = ±2 is 9, not 0, so both are vertical asymptotes.
    2. Horizontal. The degrees match (2 and 2): divide the leading coefficients, 3/1 = 3.
    3. Check the limit. limx→∞ (3 − 3/x²)/(1 − 4/x²) = 3/1 = 3. The same value at −∞.
    4. Answer. Vertical: x = 2 and x = −2. Horizontal: y = 3.

    Common mistakes

    • Calling every zero of the bottom a vertical asymptote. If the factor also cancels with the top, it is a hole.
    • Writing lim = ∞ as if ∞ were a number you can substitute.
    • Using only the leading coefficient of the top for the horizontal asymptote.
    • Forgetting the limit at −∞ can differ from +∞ (for example, ex or an odd-degree ratio).
    • Thinking a graph cannot cross its horizontal asymptote. It can, near the origin; the asymptote describes the far ends.

    Reading the sign

    To get the sign of an infinite limit, check which side you approach from. Near x = 2, 1/(x − 2) is large positive from the right (positive denominator) and large negative from the left, so limx→2⁺ = ∞ and limx→2⁻ = −∞, and the two-sided limit does not exist.

    Check yourself: limx→∞ (5x + 1)/(2x² + 7) =

    AP Unit 2AB & BC

    Average vs instantaneous rate

    Speed over a trip is easy: distance divided by time. Speed at one instant needs a limit. Watch a secant line turn into a tangent line.

    The idea

    The average rate of change of f from x = a to x = b is the slope of the secant line through the two points: (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a). It is what a car's trip computer tells you: miles per hour over the whole trip.

    The instantaneous rate of change is what the speedometer shows at one moment. Shrink the interval: move the second point toward the first. The secant line rotates and settles into the tangent line, and its slope is the limit of the average rates. That limit is the derivative.

    (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a)average rate = secant slope

    units: output per inpute.g. meters per second
    Shrink the interval
    Function
    average rate (secant slope)—
    instantaneous rate (tangent slope)—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Make h smaller and smaller on x² at a = 1. What do the secant slopes approach?

      What you should see

      Toward 2, the slope of the tangent line at x = 1. With h = 0.05 the average rate is 2.05; with h = 0.001 it would be 2.001.

    2. Set h negative (second point on the left). Does the answer still approach the same number?

      What you should see

      Yes: 1.95 from the left, 2.05 from the right. For a smooth curve both sides squeeze toward the same tangent slope.

    3. Choose eˣ at a = 0 with h = 1.2, then shrink h to 0.05. What number is the secant slope heading for?

      What you should see

      About 1.93 at h = 1.2 and 1.03 at h = 0.05, heading for 1: the slope of eˣ at 0 is e⁰ = 1. The big gap overestimates because eˣ curves upward.

    4. Choose sin x with a = 1.6 (near the top of the hump). Compare h = 0.5 with h = −0.5.

      What you should see

      About −0.27 to the right and +0.22 to the left: the two secants tilt opposite ways because they straddle the peak. The tangent slope, cos 1.6 ≈ −0.03, is nearly flat and sits between them.

    Worked example

    A car's position is s(t) = t² feet after t seconds. Find the average velocity from t = 1 to t = 3 and estimate the velocity at t = 1.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Average rate. (s(3) − s(1))/(3 − 1) = (9 − 1)/2 = 4 ft/s.
    2. Shrink the interval. From t = 1 to t = 1.1: (1.21 − 1)/0.1 = 2.1 ft/s. From 1 to 1.01: (1.0201 − 1)/0.01 = 2.01.
    3. Spot the pattern. The average velocities approach 2.
    4. Answer. Average velocity on [1, 3] is 4 ft/s; the instantaneous velocity at t = 1 is 2 ft/s.

    Worked example 2: odometer readings on a road trip (AP-style table)

    The odometer of a car on a highway trip gives the distance D(t), in miles, after t hours. (a) Find the average speed for the whole trip. (b) Estimate the car's speed at t = 1 using the readings just before t = 1, then just after. (c) Give the best estimate of the speed at t = 1 the table allows, and say what it means.

    t (hours)00.511.52
    D(t) (miles)0286185120

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. (a) Whole trip. (D(2) − D(0))/(2 − 0) = 120/2 = 60 mph. That is the slope of the long dashed secant.
    2. (b) Just before t = 1. (D(1) − D(0.5))/(1 − 0.5) = 33/0.5 = 66 mph.
    3. Just after t = 1. (D(1.5) − D(1))/(1.5 − 1) = 24/0.5 = 48 mph. The two one-sided averages disagree a lot: the car was slowing down around t = 1.
    4. (c) Center the interval. (D(1.5) − D(0.5))/(1.5 − 0.5) = 57/1 = 57 mph. It uses readings on both sides of t = 1, so it is the average of 66 and 48 and the best estimate from this table.
    5. Meaning. D′(1) ≈ 57 means that at t = 1 hour the speedometer read about 57 miles per hour. Units: miles per hour, because D is in miles and t in hours.

    Common mistakes

    • Dividing by the wrong thing: the denominator is b − a (change in input), not b.
    • Forgetting units. A rate has units of output per input, like ft/s or dollars per item.
    • Thinking the average rate over an interval equals the rate at its midpoint. It only does for special functions.
    • Using a gap h = 0 in the formula: the quotient is 0/0. A limit, not substitution.
    • With a table, using readings that do not contain the time asked about.

    Two ways to see it

    Geometrically: secant slope → tangent slope. Numerically: a table of (f(a+h) − f(a))/h for smaller and smaller h. Algebraically: simplify the quotient, then let h → 0. The next module does that last step formally.

    Check yourself: The average rate of change of f over [2, 5] is

    AP Unit 2AB & BC

    The derivative & differentiability

    The derivative is a function: at every x it gives the slope of the tangent line. Some graphs have no tangent at certain points, and those are worth knowing.

    The idea

    Define f′(x) = limh→0 (f(x + h) − f(x))/h. When this limit exists, f is differentiable at x and f′(x) is the slope of the tangent line there. Doing this at every x produces a new function f′, the derivative function, and its graph is built from the slopes of the original.

    Differentiable means smooth: no corner, no cusp, no vertical tangent, no jump. A corner has two different one-sided slopes. A vertical tangent has an infinite slope. A discontinuity has no tangent at all. Differentiable ⇒ continuous, but not the other way: |x| is continuous at 0 and not differentiable there.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    the slope was a single number you got from two points
    So we didn't need
    the slope at every x, as a function
    Now
    this is the central object of Units 2–5
    So we need
    the derivative defined by a limit, and the idea of "differentiable"
    f′(x) = limh→0 [f(x+h) − f(x)] / hdefinition
    f′(a) = limx→a [f(x) − f(a)] / (x − a)same, one point
    differentiable ⇒ continuousnot the converse
    Slope at every point
    Function
    slope from the left—
    slope from the right—
    differentiable here?—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose |x| and slide x through 0. What does the slope graph do at 0?

      What you should see

      The left slope is −1 and the right slope is +1, so there is no single slope at 0: the derivative graph jumps. A corner is not differentiable.

    2. Choose ∛x and move toward 0. What happens to the slope?

      What you should see

      The slope grows without bound as x → 0 (the tangent becomes vertical), so f′(0) does not exist even though the function is continuous.

    3. Choose x² and set x = 1. Compare the slope with 2x, then try x = 2.

      What you should see

      At x = 1 the slope is 2; at x = 2 it is 4: the slope at each point is 2x, which is the derivative graph below (a straight line through the origin).

    4. Choose the step function and slide x to 0. Is it differentiable there?

      What you should see

      No: at x = 0 the graph jumps by 2 (from −1 up to 1), so there is no tangent at all. Everywhere else the pieces are lines of slope 1, so the derivative graph is the constant 1 with a gap at 0. Not continuous there, so not differentiable (differentiable ⇒ continuous).

    Worked example

    Use the definition to find f′(x) for f(x) = x².

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Write the quotient. f′(x) = lim (f(x + h) − f(x))/h = lim ((x + h)² − x²)/h.
    2. Expand. (x + h)² − x² = 2xh + h².
    3. Factor out h. (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h (for h ≠ 0).
    4. Take the limit. limh→0 (2x + h) = 2x.
    5. Answer. f′(x) = 2x. At x = 3 the slope is 6.

    Common mistakes

    • Plugging h = 0 into the quotient before simplifying: it is 0/0.
    • Forgetting to expand (x + h)² as x² + 2xh + h².
    • Believing continuous means differentiable (|x| is the counterexample).
    • Writing f′(x) = limit "= 0" when the numerator goes to zero: the denominator goes to zero too.
    • Calling the derivative at a point a function. f′(a) is a number; f′(x) is a function.

    Notation

    f′(x), y′, dy/dx and d/dx[f(x)] all mean the same derivative. Leibniz's dy/dx reminds you it is a ratio of tiny changes (change in y over change in x). f′(a) means "evaluate the derivative function at x = a".

    Check yourself: Which function is continuous at 0 but not differentiable at 0?

    AP Unit 2AB & BC

    Power, sum & constant-multiple rules

    You will not use the limit definition every time. A few rules let you differentiate polynomials, roots and reciprocals almost instantly.

    The idea

    Power rule: d/dx [xn] = n xn−1. Bring the exponent down in front and lower the exponent by one. It works for every real n: x³, √x = x1/2, and 1/x² = x−2.

    Constants and sums: constants multiply through, (c·f)′ = c·f′, and sums differentiate term by term, (f + g)′ = f′ + g′. The derivative of a constant is 0, because a flat line has slope 0. Rewrite roots and fractions as powers first.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set n = 2 and x = 1.5. What are the formula and the graph's slope?

      What you should see

      f′(x) = 2x, so the slope at 1.5 is 3. The numeric slope agrees: the rule is the shortcut for the limit.

    2. Set n = 0.5 (a square root). What is f′ at x = 1?

      What you should see

      f′(x) = ½x−1/2 = 1/(2√x), so f′(1) = 0.5. The square root flattens as x grows.

    3. Set n = −1 and x = 1. What are f and the slope?

      What you should see

      f(1) = 1 and f′(x) = −x−2, so the slope is −1. The negative exponent gives a falling curve: 1/x always slopes down, steeply near 0.

    4. Set n = 1. What is the slope at every x, and why?

      What you should see

      Always 1: f(x) = x is a line of slope 1, and n·xn−1 = 1·x⁰ = 1. Try n = 0 as well: the slope is 0 because f = 1 is flat.

    5. On the polynomial lab with the starting coefficients, slide the point to x = 1.7. What is the slope, and what is happening to the cubic?

      What you should see

      f′(x) = 1.5x² − 2x − 1, so f′(1.7) = 4.335 − 3.4 − 1 = −0.065, almost 0. The tangent is nearly flat because the cubic is at its local minimum (exactly at x ≈ 1.72).

    Worked example

    Differentiate f(x) = 4x³ − 6√x + 5/x² + 7.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Rewrite as powers. f(x) = 4x³ − 6x1/2 + 5x−2 + 7.
    2. Differentiate each term. 4·3x² = 12x²; −6·(1/2)x−1/2 = −3x−1/2; 5·(−2)x−3 = −10x−3; the constant 7 goes to 0.
    3. Answer. f′(x) = 12x² − 3x−1/2 − 10x−3, or 12x² − 3/√x − 10/x³.

    Common mistakes

    • Differentiating a constant as if it had an x: the derivative of 7 is 0, and of 7x is 7.
    • Forgetting to lower the exponent, writing (x³)′ = 3x³.
    • Applying the power rule to eˣ or 2ˣ. The variable is in the exponent there: a different rule.
    • Not rewriting 1/x² or √x as powers before differentiating.
    • Splitting a product or quotient term by term. (x²·x³)′ is not (x²)′·(x³)′.

    Why it works

    The derivative of x² is 2x (you saw it from the definition). For x³ expand (x + h)³ = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³, subtract x³, divide by h and let h → 0: 3x². The pattern n xn−1 comes from the binomial expansion, and it holds for every real n.

    AP Unit 2AB & BC

    Trig, e^x and ln x derivatives

    Four functions to memorize once: the slopes of sine, cosine, ex and ln x.

    The idea

    Here is the pattern worth seeing. The slope of sin x is cos x: sine climbs fastest at 0 (slope 1 = cos 0) and is flat at its peaks (slope 0 = cos π/2). The slope of cos x is −sin x: cosine starts flat, then falls. The slope of ex is ex: the one function whose slope equals its height. The slope of ln x is 1/x: steep near 0, flatter and flatter after.

    tan x, cot x, sec x and csc x follow from the quotient rule. The three with "co" in their names get minus signs. These derivatives need radians.

      At the peak (x = π/2) the tangent is flat, so f′ = 0, and cos(π/2) = 0. The slope graph is the cosine curve.

    2. Choose eˣ and tick the box. What do you notice about the two graphs?

      They are identical. Wherever the curve has height h its slope is h too. That is what makes e special.

    3. Choose ln x and compare the slope at x = 0.2 with the slope at x = 3.

      f′ = 1/x, so the slope is 5 at x = 0.2 (steep) and 1/3 at x = 3 (gentle). The log curve flattens as x grows but keeps rising.

    4. Choose tan x and slide x toward π/2 ≈ 1.57. What happens to the slope?

      f′ = sec²x: at x = 1 it is about 3.43, and it grows without bound as x → π/2, where the tangent line becomes vertical (tan x has a vertical asymptote there).

    Worked example

    Differentiate f(x) = 3 sin x − 2ex + 5 ln x, and find f′(1).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Term by term. (3 sin x)′ = 3 cos x; (−2ex)′ = −2ex; (5 ln x)′ = 5/x.
    2. Combine. f′(x) = 3 cos x − 2ex + 5/x.
    3. Evaluate at 1. 3 cos 1 − 2e + 5 = 3(0.5403) − 2(2.7183) + 5 = 1.6209 − 5.4366 + 5 ≈ 1.184 (radians).

    Common mistakes

    • Writing (cos x)′ = sin x. The sign is minus: −sin x.
    • Using degrees on the calculator. The rules assume radians.
    • Writing (ex)′ = x ex−1. The power rule needs the variable in the base.
    • Writing (ln x)′ = ln x or x. It is 1/x.
    • Forgetting (ax)′ = ax ln a for other bases.

    The other trig derivatives

    (tan x)′ = sec²x, (cot x)′ = −csc²x, (sec x)′ = sec x tan x, (csc x)′ = −csc x cot x. You can get all of them from the quotient rule on sin and cos, but they are common enough to memorize.

    Check yourself: (cos x)′ =

    AP Unit 2AB & BC

    Product & quotient rules

    The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives. Here is what it is, and why the naive answer fails.

    The idea

    If f = u·v, change in f has two parts: u changes while v stays, and v changes while u stays. That gives (uv)′ = u′v + uv′: "derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second". For a quotient, (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²: low d-high minus high d-low over low squared.

    You can check that (uv)′ ≠ u′v′ with any example: for u = v = x, uv = x² has derivative 2x, but u′v′ = 1. Watch the lab: the naive answer drifts away from the true slope.

    3. Choose x²·sin x at x = 1.5. Product rule against the naive u′v′.

      What you should see

      Product rule: 2x sin x + x² cos x = 3(0.9975) + 2.25(0.0707) ≈ 3.152, matching the numeric slope. The naive u′v′ = 2x cos x ≈ 0.212 is far off.

    4. Choose (x² + 1)/(x − 1) at x = 2. Compare the quotient rule with u′/v′.

      What you should see

      Quotient rule: (2x(x − 1) − (x² + 1))/(x − 1)² = (4 − 5)/1 = −1, matching the numeric slope (the curve is falling there). The naive u′/v′ = 2x/1 = 4 has the wrong sign.

    Worked example

    Differentiate f(x) = x² eˣ and g(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 2).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Product rule on f. u = x², v = eˣ, so u′ = 2x, v′ = eˣ. f′ = 2x·eˣ + x²·eˣ = eˣ(x² + 2x).
    2. Quotient rule on g. u = x + 1, v = x − 2, so u′ = 1, v′ = 1. g′ = (1·(x − 2) − (x + 1)·1)/(x − 2)².
    3. Simplify the top. (x − 2) − (x + 1) = −3.
    4. Answer. f′(x) = eˣ(x² + 2x) and g′(x) = −3/(x − 2)².

    Common mistakes

    • Writing (uv)′ = u′v′. It misses half of the change.
    • Getting the quotient numerator in the wrong order: it is u′v − uv′ (low d-high minus high d-low).
    • Forgetting to square the denominator.
    • Using the quotient rule when the denominator is a constant. Just pull the constant out.
    • Not simplifying: factor and cancel if you can.

    Why the product rule has two terms

    A rectangle with sides u and v has area uv. If both sides grow, the area gains a strip along each side: u′v from stretching one side and uv′ from stretching the other. The tiny corner u′v′ is second order and vanishes in the limit.

    Check yourself: d/dx [x sin x] =

    AP Unit 3AB & BC

    The chain rule

    When one function sits inside another, rates multiply: the speed of the outer function times the speed of the inner one.

    The idea

    Picture a chain of gears. If gear A turns 3 times as fast as gear B, and gear B turns twice as fast as gear C, then A turns 3 × 2 = 6 times as fast as C. A composite function y = f(g(x)) works the same way: as x changes, u = g(x) changes at rate g′(x), and y changes with u at rate f′(u). Multiply them.

    So d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x): differentiate the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. Leibniz writes it so it looks like cancelling: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx).

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    each rule handled one function at a time
    So we didn't need
    a way through nested functions
    Now
    sin(x²), e^{3x}, (2x + 1)⁵ and √(x² + 1) all need it
    So we need
    the chain rule
    (f∘g)′(x) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x)chain rule
    dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx)Leibniz form
    d/dx [f(u)] = f′(u) · u′shorthand
    Two rates, multiplied
    Composite

    g′(x): inner rate—
    f′(g(x)): outer rate—
    product—
    numeric slope of f(g(x))—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose e²ˣ. What are the two rates at any x, and what do they give?

      What you should see

      The inner rate is always 2, the outer rate is e2x: the product 2e2x matches the numeric slope. The factor 2 is what the chain rule adds.

    2. Choose (3x+1)⁴ and change x. Which factor is always the same?

      What you should see

      The inner rate 3. The outer rate 4u³ depends on x, but the inner rate does not, so the derivative is 4(3x+1)³·3 = 12(3x + 1)³.

    3. Choose sin(x²) and slide x to 1.25. What is the slope, and why so small?

      What you should see

      f′ = 2x cos(x²) ≈ 2.5·cos(1.5625) ≈ 0.021, nearly 0. At x = 1.25 the inner value x² ≈ 1.56 is almost π/2, where sin u peaks, so the outer rate cos u is nearly 0 and the product is too.

    4. Choose √(x² + 1) and slide x to 0. Which factor makes the slope 0 there?

      What you should see

      The inner rate 2x is 0 at x = 0, so the product is 0: f′ = x/√(x² + 1) = 0, a minimum at (0, 1). At x = 0.8 the slope is 0.8/√1.64 ≈ 0.625.

    Worked example

    Differentiate f(x) = sin(x²) and g(x) = (3x + 1)⁵.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Name the layers. For f: outer = sin u, inner = u = x². For g: outer = u⁵, inner = u = 3x + 1.
    2. Differentiate the outside, keep the inside. f′ = cos(x²) · (x²)′. g′ = 5(3x + 1)⁴ · (3x + 1)′.
    3. Multiply by the derivative of the inside. (x²)′ = 2x and (3x + 1)′ = 3.
    4. Answer. f′(x) = 2x cos(x²); g′(x) = 15(3x + 1)⁴.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting the inside derivative: (sin x²)′ is not cos x².
    • Changing the inside when differentiating the outside. cos(x²) keeps x² as it is.
    • Applying the power rule to eˣ-type functions: (e3x)′ = 3e3x, not 3x e3x−1.
    • Stopping early on layers: √(sin(x²)) has three layers.
    • Mixing up the order of composition when evaluating at a point: you need g(a) first, then f′(g(a)).

    Several layers

    For three layers, y = f(g(h(x))), multiply three rates: f′(g(h(x)))·g′(h(x))·h′(x). Work from the outside in, one layer at a time, and write each step.

    Check yourself: d/dx [ex²] =

    AP Unit 3AB & BC

    Implicit differentiation

    Some curves, like a circle, cannot be written as y = f(x). You can still find their slopes by differentiating both sides and treating y as a function of x.

    The idea

    The circle x² + y² = 25 is not a single function (each x has two y values), but near any point it behaves like one. Differentiate both sides with respect to x. The key: whenever you differentiate something with y in it, use the chain rule and write dy/dx, because y depends on x.

    For the circle: 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y. The slope depends on both x and y: you need the point. At (3, 4) the slope is −3/4: the tangent heads down to the right, as a circle does in its upper right.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    y was always given as a formula in x
    So we didn't need
    a way to find slopes of curves without solving for y
    Now
    circles, ellipses and any equation tangled in x and y
    So we need
    implicit differentiation: differentiate, treat y as y(x), solve for dy/dx
    d/dx [y²] = 2y · dy/dxchain rule on y
    d/dx [xy] = y + x · dy/dxproduct rule
    solve for dy/dxcollect the dy/dx terms
    A slope you can see
    Curve

    point (x, y)—
    dy/dx from the formula—
    slope measured on the curve—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On the circle, move to x = 3 on the upper branch. What is the slope?

      What you should see

      At x = 2.4 the point is (2.4, 1.8), and dy/dx = −x/y = −2.4/1.8 = −1.33. The tangent falls to the right.

    2. Switch to the lower branch at the same x. What happens to the slope?

      What you should see

      y is now negative, so −x/y is positive: the lower right of a circle slopes up. Same x, opposite slope, because the formula needs y too.

    3. Choose the ellipse x² + 4y² = 4 and use x = 1 on the upper branch. What is the slope?

      What you should see

      y = √3/2 ≈ 0.866, and dy/dx = −x/(4y) = −1/(2√3) ≈ −0.289. A gentle downward slope, since the upper right of an ellipse that is wider than tall is nearly flat there.

    4. Choose xy = 4 at x = 2. What is the slope, and does the sign depend on the branch?

      What you should see

      The point is (2, 2) and dy/dx = −y/x = −1. On the other branch (x < 0, y < 0) it is also negative: −y/x is negative whenever x and y have the same sign, so both branches always fall.

    5. Choose y² = x³ − x + 1 and set x = −1.25 (upper branch). What happens to the slope as x approaches the left end?

      What you should see

      The point is about (−1.25, 0.545) and dy/dx = (3x² − 1)/(2y) ≈ 3.38. As x → −1.3247 the curve reaches y = 0, the denominator 2y goes to 0 and the slope blows up: a vertical tangent at the left tip.

    Worked example

    Find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25 and the slope at (3, 4). Then find dy/dx for x²y + y³ = 10.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Differentiate both sides. d/dx[x²] + d/dx[y²] = d/dx[25] gives 2x + 2y·y′ = 0.
    2. Solve for y′. 2y·y′ = −2x, so y′ = −x/y. At (3, 4): −3/4.
    3. Second curve, product rule on x²y. 2xy + x²y′ + 3y²y′ = 0.
    4. Collect the y′ terms. y′(x² + 3y²) = −2xy.
    5. Answer. y′ = −2xy/(x² + 3y²).

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting dy/dx after differentiating a y term: (y²)′ is 2y·y′, not 2y.
    • Not using the product rule on mixed terms like xy.
    • Dropping y from the answer. Leave it in; the formula depends on both coordinates.
    • Not isolating dy/dx: collect every y′ term on one side, factor and divide.
    • Substituting the point too early. Differentiate first, then substitute.

    Why it works

    Near a point on the curve, y is some function of x, even if you cannot write it down. Differentiating an equation that is true for all nearby (x, y) gives another true equation. The chain rule is just the way to differentiate y² = (y(x))² with respect to x.

    Check yourself: d/dx [y³] with respect to x equals

    AP Unit 3AB & BC

    Inverse functions & inverse trig

    If f turns a into b, its inverse turns b back into a. Their slopes at matching points are reciprocals, and that fact gives the derivatives of ln, arcsin and arctan.

    The idea

    The graph of f⁻¹ is the graph of f reflected over the line y = x. A reflection swaps the roles of rise and run, so a tangent of slope m at (a, b) becomes a tangent of slope 1/m at (b, a). That is the rule: (f⁻¹)′(b) = 1 / f′(a) where f(a) = b.

    Use it on f(x) = sin x to get (arcsin x)′ = 1/√(1 − x²), and on tan x to get (arctan x)′ = 1/(1 + x²). The AP course asks for arcsin, arccos and arctan.

    Now

    (arcsin x)′ = 1/√(1−x²)−1/√(1−x²) for arccos
    (arctan x)′ = 1/(1+x²)
    Reflect a tangent line
    Function

    (f⁻¹)′(f(a))—
    product—
    Inverse trig derivatives
    Function

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On eˣ, find the product f′(a)·(f⁻¹)′.

      What you should see

      Always 1: the slopes are reciprocals. At a = 0.6, f′ = e^0.6 ≈ 1.82, and the inverse (ln) has slope 1/1.82 ≈ 0.55 at the matching point.

    2. On arcsin x, move x toward 1. What happens to the slope?

      What you should see

      It grows large: arcsin has a vertical tangent at x = 1, matching 1/√(1 − x²) → ∞. The sine curve is flat there, so its inverse is steep.

    3. On sin x, set a = 1.5, close to π/2. What is the inverse slope?

      What you should see

      f′(1.5) = cos 1.5 ≈ 0.0707, so the inverse slope is 1/0.0707 ≈ 14.1. Where sine is nearly flat its inverse is nearly vertical, the same fact as arcsin′ blowing up at x = 1.

    4. On x³ + x, set a = 1. What is (f⁻¹)′(2)?

      What you should see

      f(1) = 2 and f′(1) = 3 + 1 = 4, so (f⁻¹)′(2) = 1/4. The product of the two slopes is 1 again.

    5. On arctan x, slide x from 0 to 0.9. Where is the slope largest?

      What you should see

      At x = 0: 1/(1 + 0²) = 1. It falls as |x| grows (0.8 at x = 0.5, about 0.55 at x = 0.9), because arctan levels off toward ±π/2 for large inputs.

    Worked example

    If f(x) = x³ + x, find (f⁻¹)′(10).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Find a. We need f(a) = 10. Try a = 2: 8 + 2 = 10. ✓
    2. Differentiate f. f′(x) = 3x² + 1, so f′(2) = 13.
    3. Reciprocal. (f⁻¹)′(10) = 1/f′(2).
    4. Answer. 1/13.

    Common mistakes

    • Evaluating f′ at b instead of at a. You need the x that f sends to b.
    • Writing (f⁻¹)′ = 1/f′(x) without the inverse in the argument: it is 1/f′(f⁻¹(b)).
    • Confusing f⁻¹ with 1/f.
    • Forgetting the domain restrictions for inverse trig.
    • Dropping the chain rule: d/dx arctan(2x) = 2/(1 + 4x²), not 1/(1 + 4x²).

    Why arcsin has that derivative

    Let y = arcsin x, so sin y = x. Differentiate implicitly: cos y · y′ = 1, so y′ = 1/cos y. With y between −π/2 and π/2, cos y = √(1 − sin²y) = √(1 − x²).

    Check yourself: If f(2) = 5 and f′(2) = 4, then (f⁻¹)′(5) =

    AP Unit 3AB & BC

    Higher-order derivatives & choosing a rule

    Differentiate again and you get the rate at which the slope changes. Then practise the skill that matters most on the exam: picking the right rule.

    The idea

    The second derivative f″ is the derivative of f′. If f is position, f′ is velocity and f″ is acceleration. If f′ is slope, f″ tells you how the slope is changing: positive means the slope is increasing (the curve bends up), negative means it bends down. You will use this in Unit 5 to find concavity.

    With more rules, the real skill is choosing. Look at the outermost operation first: is the whole expression a sum, a product, a quotient, or a function of something? That operation is the rule you apply first.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    one derivative per function
    So we didn't need
    f″, f‴ and a method for picking the right rule
    Now
    acceleration, concavity and the shapes of graphs
    So we need
    repeated differentiation, and a decision procedure
    f″ = (f′)′second derivative
    d²y/dx² · f⁽ⁿ⁾notation
    sum → product → quotient → chainlook at the outermost operation first
    Height, slope and bend
    Function
    f(x): height—
    f′(x): slope—
    f″(x): bend—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose x³ − 3x and slide x to 0. What is f″ there, and what does the curve do?

      What you should see

      f″(0) = 0: the bend switches there. The curve changes from bending down (f″ < 0 for x < 0) to bending up (f″ > 0).

    2. Choose sin x. Where is f″ largest in size?

      What you should see

      At the peak (x = π/2): f″ = −sin(π/2) = −1. The curve bends sharply there, and f′ passes through zero.

    3. Choose x⁴ − 2x² and set x = 0. What do f′ and f″ say?

      What you should see

      f′(0) = 0 (a flat tangent) and f″(0) = −4 < 0: bending down at a flat point, so x = 0 is a local maximum of f (the top of the middle hump).

    4. Choose eˣ and look at the three readouts at x = 0.5.

      What you should see

      All three are e^0.5 ≈ 1.6487: eˣ is its own derivative, so f = f′ = f″ at every x. The curve is always rising and always bending up.

    5. Choose x³ − 3x and set x = 1. Which derivative tells you it is a minimum?

      What you should see

      f′(1) = 0 says the tangent is flat; f″(1) = 6 > 0 says the curve bends up there. Together: a local minimum, f(1) = −2.

    Worked example

    Find f″(x) for f(x) = x e2x.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Choose a rule. It is a product of x and e2x.
    2. First derivative. f′ = 1·e2x + x·(2e2x) = e2x(1 + 2x).
    3. Differentiate again (product). f″ = 2e2x(1 + 2x) + e2x·2.
    4. Simplify. f″ = e2x(2 + 4x + 2) = e2x(4x + 4).

    Common mistakes

    • Differentiating the original instead of f′ for the second derivative.
    • Not simplifying f′ before differentiating again.
    • Choosing the wrong rule: look at the outermost operation, not the innermost.
    • Confusing f² with f″.
    • Sign errors when differentiating trig functions twice: sin → cos → −sin.

    Which rule first?

    Sum or difference: split and differentiate each term. Product of two functions of x: product rule. Quotient: quotient rule (or rewrite as a product with a negative power). A function of a function, like sin(3x) or √(x² + 1): chain rule. Constant times something: pull out the constant. Many problems need two or three of these in order.

    Check yourself: Which rule do you apply first to f(x) = x² sin(3x)?

    AP Unit 4AB & BC

    Derivatives in context & motion

    A derivative is a rate, and every rate has units and a story. The classic story: a particle moving along a line.

    The idea

    If s(t) is position, then v(t) = s′(t) is velocity and a(t) = v′(t) = s″(t) is acceleration. Velocity can be negative (moving left or down). Speed is the size of velocity, |v|. The units of each derivative are the units of the quantity divided by the units of time: meters, meters per second, meters per second squared.

    The particle is at rest when v = 0, and it can turn around only there. It is speeding up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign, and slowing down when the signs are opposite. This is the sign test the exam loves.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    a derivative was a slope on a graph
    So we didn't need
    a meaning: the instantaneous rate of change of a real quantity, with units
    Now
    motion, growth, flow, cost and everything that changes in time
    So we need
    velocity, speed and acceleration, and how to interpret their signs
    v = s′ , a = v′ = s″velocity, acceleration
    speed = |v|always ≥ 0
    v and a same sign → speeding upopposite signs → slowing down
    A particle on a line
    Motion
    position s—
    velocity v—
    acceleration a—
    what the particle is doing—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose the first motion and set t = 2.5. Is the particle speeding up or slowing down?

      What you should see

      v(2.5) = 3(1.5)(−0.5) = −2.25 and a(2.5) = 6(2.5) − 12 = 3. Opposite signs, so it is slowing down: moving left, but being pushed right.

    2. Choose the ball (s = 20t − 5t²) and set t = 2. What does v = 0 mean here?

      What you should see

      At t = 2 the ball is at its highest point (s = 20): it has stopped for an instant before falling. Velocity changes sign there, and acceleration is −10 the whole time.

    3. First motion again, t = 1. The particle is at rest. Does it stay there?

      What you should see

      No. At t = 1, s = 4 and v = 0, but a = −6: it is being pushed left, so it turns around and heads back. v = 0 is a turning point, not a stop.

    4. First motion, t = 2. Acceleration is 0. What is special about the velocity there?

      What you should see

      v(2) = −3 is the lowest velocity between t = 1 and t = 3, so the particle is moving left fastest (speed 3). a = v′ = 0 marks a minimum of v, just as f′ = 0 marks a min of f.

    5. Choose the spring (s = 3 sin t) and set t = 1.56, just before π/2 ≈ 1.571. Where is the mass, and which way is it pushed?

      What you should see

      Almost at the far end: s ≈ 3, v ≈ 0.03 (nearly stopped) and a ≈ −3, so it is slowing down. At t = π/2 it stops and turns back. The spring pulls hardest at the ends, where the mass is momentarily stopped: a = −s for this motion.

    Worked example

    A particle has position s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t for t ≥ 0. When is it at rest, and is it speeding up or slowing down at t = 2.5?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Velocity. v(t) = s′(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3).
    2. At rest. v = 0 at t = 1 and t = 3.
    3. Acceleration. a(t) = v′(t) = 6t − 12.
    4. Signs at t = 2.5. v(2.5) = 3(1.5)(−0.5) = −2.25 and a(2.5) = 3.
    5. Answer. At rest at t = 1 and t = 3. At t = 2.5 velocity is negative and acceleration positive (opposite signs), so the particle is slowing down.

    Worked example 2: a train on a straight track (AP-style table)

    A train moves along a straight east–west track. Its velocity v(t), in meters per minute (positive means east), is a differentiable function of time, with the values shown in the table. (a) Estimate the train's acceleration at t = 3.5 minutes, with units. (b) Must the train be at rest at some time between t = 5 and t = 8? Explain. (c) At t = 8 the acceleration is −15 m/min². Is the train speeding up or slowing down then?

    t (minutes)025812
    v(t) (meters per minute)010040−120−150

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. (a) Use the readings on either side of 3.5. a(3.5) = v′(3.5) ≈ (v(5) − v(2))/(5 − 2) = (40 − 100)/3 = −20 m/min². Units: (m/min) per minute.
    2. Meaning. Around t = 3.5 the train's velocity is dropping by about 20 m/min every minute. It is still moving east (v > 0) but braking.
    3. (b) Yes. v is differentiable, so it is continuous. v(5) = 40 > 0 and v(8) = −120 < 0, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem v(c) = 0 for some c between 5 and 8. At that moment the train is at rest, and it turns around to head west.
    4. (c) Compare signs. At t = 8, v = −120 (moving west) and a = −15. Both are negative.
    5. Answer (c). Same signs, so the train is speeding up: its speed |v| is growing. Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down.

    Common mistakes

    • Confusing velocity with speed: velocity has a sign, speed does not.
    • Saying the particle is speeding up whenever acceleration is positive. You must compare it with the sign of velocity.
    • Forgetting units. Always write them: m/s, m/s².
    • Treating v = 0 as a stop forever. It may only be a turning point.
    • Using the position formula to find velocity at a time without differentiating first.
    • With a table, estimating a derivative from readings that do not surround the time asked about.

    Reading the story

    Positive velocity means moving in the positive direction; negative means the opposite. Where velocity changes sign the particle turns around. Where acceleration is zero velocity is momentarily constant (a maximum or minimum of v). The same logic reads any rate: if V(t) is volume, V′(t) is a flow rate, and V′ > 0 means filling.

    AP Unit 4AB & BC

    Related rates

    When two quantities are tied together by an equation and both change in time, their rates are tied together too.

    The idea

    A ladder slides down a wall. The foot moves out at a steady 2 ft/s, but the top does not move down at a steady rate: it starts slowly and speeds up. The lengths x and y are linked by x² + y² = L², so their rates are linked by the derivative of that equation with respect to time.

    The method: draw and label; write an equation that holds at every moment; differentiate with respect to t (chain rule on every variable); only then substitute the numbers of the moment you care about. Substituting before differentiating freezes the variables and gives 0.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On the ladder (10 ft, foot moving out at 2 ft/s) set x = 6. How fast is the top sliding down?

      What you should see

      y = 8, and dy/dt = −(x/y)(2) = −(6/8)(2) = −1.5 ft/s: the top drops 1.5 ft/s.

    2. Now slide x up to 9. What happens to the speed of the top?

      What you should see

      y ≈ 4.36 and dy/dt ≈ −4.13 ft/s: it speeds up a lot as the ladder nears the floor, even though the foot moves at a steady 2 ft/s.

    3. Keep x = 6 and double the given rate to 4 ft/s. Predict the new dy/dt before you look.

      What you should see

      dy/dt = −(6/8)(4) = −3 ft/s, exactly double. At a fixed moment the rate you want is proportional to the given rate; only the moment (x and y) sets the factor.

    4. Choose the lamppost. Drag the person from 5 ft to 25 ft from the pole. Does the shadow grow faster when the person is far away?

      What you should see

      No. The shadow grows at 10/3 ≈ 3.33 ft/s and its tip moves at 25/3 ≈ 8.33 ft/s wherever the person is, because similar triangles make s = (2/3)x, a straight-line relationship.

    5. Choose the cone tank (water in at 2 ft³/min). Compare dh/dt at h = 2 ft and at h = 8 ft.

      What you should see

      About 0.995 ft/min at h = 2 but only 0.062 ft/min at h = 8, 16 times slower: the surface is 4 times wider, so its area is 16 times bigger, and the same water spreads over it.

    Worked example

    A 10 ft ladder leans on a wall. Its foot slides away at 2 ft/s. How fast is the top sliding down when the foot is 6 ft from the wall?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Draw and equation. x = distance of foot from wall, y = height of top: x² + y² = 100.
    2. Differentiate with respect to t. 2x·dx/dt + 2y·dy/dt = 0, so dy/dt = −(x/y)·dx/dt.
    3. Substitute the moment. x = 6 gives y = √(100 − 36) = 8, and dx/dt = 2.
    4. Compute. dy/dt = −(6/8)(2) = −1.5.
    5. Answer. The top is sliding down at 1.5 ft/s (dy/dt = −1.5 ft/s).

    Worked example 2: a shadow on the sidewalk

    A street light is at the top of a 15 ft pole. A person 6 ft tall walks away from the pole at 5 ft/s. (a) How fast is the person's shadow getting longer when they are 40 ft from the pole? (b) How fast is the tip of the shadow moving?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Draw and name. x = distance from the pole to the person, s = length of the shadow. The tip of the shadow is x + s from the pole. Given: dx/dt = 5 ft/s.
    2. Equation that holds at every moment. The big triangle (pole, ground to the tip) and the small one (person, shadow) are similar: 15/(x + s) = 6/s. Cross-multiply: 15s = 6x + 6s, so 9s = 6x and s = (2/3)x.
    3. (a) Differentiate in t. ds/dt = (2/3)·dx/dt = (2/3)(5) = 10/3 ≈ 3.33 ft/s.
    4. (b) The tip. The tip is at D = x + s = (5/3)x, so dD/dt = (5/3)(5) = 25/3 ≈ 8.33 ft/s. The tip outruns the person because the shadow is growing too.
    5. What about the 40 ft? Neither answer depends on x: s is a constant multiple of x, so its rate is too. AP problems sometimes give a value you do not need; say so rather than forcing it in.

    Common mistakes

    • Substituting numbers before differentiating. Constants have derivative 0, so you lose the rates.
    • Forgetting dx/dt: 2x alone is not d/dt of x².
    • Treating a changing quantity as constant (for example the ladder's length is constant, but x and y are not).
    • Ignoring signs: a decreasing quantity has a negative rate. Report it with the right direction.
    • Dropping units. Rates have units of quantity per time.
    • In shadow problems, using the distance to the person when the question asks about the tip of the shadow (x + s).

    A checklist

    Name every variable with units. Write what is constant and what changes. Use a relationship that is true at all times (Pythagoras, similar triangles, a volume or area formula), not just at the moment asked about. Differentiate. Substitute known values. Solve. Include units and a sentence.

    Check yourself: A circle's radius grows at 2 cm/s. dA/dt = ?

    AP Unit 4AB & BC

    Linearization & differentials

    Zoom in far enough and a curve is a line. Use the tangent line to estimate values you cannot compute by hand.

    The idea

    Near x = a, the curve is almost indistinguishable from its tangent line L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a). So to estimate f at a nearby point, use L instead: f(x) ≈ L(x). This is how a calculator first estimates square roots, and how physicists replace sin θ by θ for small angles.

    Whether the estimate is too big or too small depends on bending. If the curve is concave down (f″ < 0) the tangent line lies above the curve: the estimate is an overestimate. If concave up (f″ > 0) the tangent lies below: an underestimate. Differentials write the same idea as dy = f′(x) dx.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    a function value needed a calculator or a formula
    So we didn't need
    a fast, local approximation
    Now
    estimating √ and trig values, error propagation and later Taylor polynomials
    So we need

    dy = f′(x) dxdifferential

    true f(x)—

    the tangent line is—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On √x with a = 1, estimate √1.2.

      What you should see

      L(x) = 1 + ½(x − 1), so L(1.2) = 1.1. The true √1.2 = 1.0954: a tiny overestimate, because √x is concave down.

    2. Slide x far from a. What happens to the error?

      What you should see

      The error grows quickly: L(4) = 2.5 but √4 = 2. A tangent line is only a good estimate close to a.

    3. Choose ln x with a = 1 and estimate ln 1.1. Over or under?

      What you should see

      L(x) = x − 1, so L(1.1) = 0.1, while ln 1.1 ≈ 0.0953. An overestimate, because ln x is concave down.

    4. Choose eˣ with a = 1 and estimate e1.4. Over or under?

      What you should see

      L(1.4) = e + e(0.4) = 1.4e ≈ 3.8056, but e1.4 ≈ 4.0552: an underestimate by about 0.25, because eˣ is concave up. A bigger step and stronger bending give a bigger error.

    Worked example

    Use a linearization to estimate √26.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Pick a nearby easy point. f(x) = √x, a = 25 (since √25 = 5).
    2. Slope. f′(x) = 1/(2√x), so f′(25) = 1/10.
    3. Build L. L(x) = 5 + (1/10)(x − 25).
    4. Estimate. L(26) = 5 + 0.1 = 5.1.
    5. Answer. √26 ≈ 5.1 (true value 5.0990). Overestimate, since √x is concave down.

    Worked example 2: snow depth (AP-style table)

    During a snowstorm, the depth of snow on the ground is d(t) inches, t hours after midnight. d is twice differentiable, with selected values in the table. Also d′(7) = 0.5 and d″(t) < 0 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8. (a) Use the data to estimate d′(6), with units. (b) Use the line tangent to the graph of d at t = 7 to estimate the depth at t = 8. (c) Is your estimate in (b) an overestimate or an underestimate? Explain.

    t (hours)0257
    d(t) (inches)4.06.69.611.0

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. (a) Use the two readings around t = 6: d′(6) ≈ (d(7) − d(5))/(7 − 5) = (11.0 − 9.6)/2 = 0.7 inch per hour.
    2. (b) Tangent line. At t = 7 the point is (7, 11.0) and the slope is d′(7) = 0.5: L(t) = 11.0 + 0.5(t − 7).
    3. Estimate. d(8) ≈ L(8) = 11.0 + 0.5(1) = 11.5 inches.
    4. (c) d″(t) < 0, so the graph of d is concave down and lies below its tangent line. The estimate 11.5 is an overestimate.
    5. Check against the table. The slopes between readings are (6.6 − 4.0)/2 = 1.3, (9.6 − 6.6)/3 = 1.0 and 0.7 inch per hour: decreasing, as a concave-down d should be, and d′(7) = 0.5 continues the trend. The snow is still piling up, just more slowly.

    Common mistakes

    • Choosing a not close to x. The estimate is only good near a.
    • Evaluating f′ at x instead of at a.
    • Forgetting f(a) in L(x).
    • Saying overestimate/underestimate from the sign of f′. It depends on f″ (concavity).
    • Using degrees for trig linearizations. They require radians.
    • With a table, estimating a derivative from readings that do not surround the point when ones that do are available.

    Differentials

    The change in y along the tangent line is dy = f′(x) dx, while the true change is Δy. For a small dx they nearly agree. This is how measurement error spreads: if the radius of a sphere is measured with a small error dr, the error in volume is about dV = 4πr² dr.

    Check yourself: The tangent line to f at a lies above the curve near a when

    AP Unit 4AB & BC

    L'Hôpital's rule

    If a limit of a ratio is 0/0 or ∞/∞, you can differentiate the top and bottom separately and try again.

    The idea

    When both f and g go to 0 at a, the ratio f/g depends on how fast each goes to 0. Near a, f ≈ f′(a)(x − a) and g ≈ g′(a)(x − a), so their ratio is about f′(a)/g′(a): the ratio of their rates. That is L'Hôpital's rule: lim f/g = lim f′/g′, if the left side is 0/0 or ∞/∞ and the right side exists.

    Check the form first. Never apply the rule to something that is not 0/0 or ∞/∞. Other indeterminate forms (0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 1∞) must be rewritten into a ratio first. You differentiate top and bottom separately: this is not the quotient rule.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    0/0 was solved by algebra when we were lucky

    a general tool for indeterminate quotients
    Now
    limits like sin x / x, (eˣ − 1)/x, x² / eˣ and ln x / x
    So we need
    L'Hôpital's rule
    lim f/g = lim f′/g′if 0/0 or ∞/∞
    0/0 · ∞/∞the two direct forms
    0·∞ · ∞−∞ · 1^∞rewrite first
    Ratio of functions vs ratio of derivatives
    Limit

    f(x)/g(x) at the probe—
    f′(x)/g′(x) at the probe—
    the limit—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose (eˣ − 1)/x and zoom in. Compare the two ratios.

      What you should see

      Both head to 1. The ratio of derivatives, eˣ/1, is already 1 at x = 0, so L'Hôpital gives the limit in one line.

    2. Choose x²/eˣ and widen the window. Which grows faster, top or bottom?

      What you should see

      The exponential wins: the ratio heads to 0. Applying the rule twice: x²/eˣ → 2x/eˣ → 2/eˣ → 0.

    3. Choose (1 − cos x)/x² and zoom in. What does the ratio do, and what does f′/g′ do?

      What you should see

      Both curves head to 1/2. The first derivative ratio, sin x/(2x), is still 0/0 at 0, so the rule is used a second time: cos x/2 → 1/2. “Still 0/0” means keep going, not stop.

    4. Choose ln x/(x − 1) at 1. What does f′/g′ look like at the point?

      What you should see

      f′/g′ = (1/x)/1 = 1/x, which equals 1 at x = 1. The dashed curve passes straight through the answer while the ratio itself has a hole there. The limit is 1.

    5. Choose sin(3x)/x. Predict the limit before you zoom in.

      What you should see

      3: the rule gives 3cos(3x)/1 → 3. The factor 3 comes from the chain rule on the top. Compare with sin x/x, whose limit is 1.

    Worked example

    Find limx→0 (1 − cos x)/x².

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Check the form. 1 − cos 0 = 0 and 0² = 0: the form 0/0, so the rule applies.
    2. Differentiate top and bottom. (sin x)/(2x).
    3. Check again. Still 0/0 at x = 0, so apply the rule once more.
    4. Differentiate again. (cos x)/2, which at x = 0 is 1/2.
    5. Answer. The limit is 1/2.

    Common mistakes

    • Using the quotient rule on f/g. Differentiate the top and bottom separately.
    • Applying the rule when the form is not 0/0 or ∞/∞ (for example 1/0 or 0/5).
    • Stopping after one step when the form is still 0/0.
    • Applying it to 0·∞ or ∞ − ∞ directly. Rewrite as a quotient first.
    • Concluding the original limit does not exist because f′/g′ oscillates: then the rule gives no information.

    Growth rates

    L'Hôpital settles a hierarchy: as x → ∞, ln x grows slower than any power of x, which grows slower than any exponential. So (ln x)/x → 0 and xn/ex → 0 for every n.

    Check yourself: Which is the first step for limx→0 sin(3x)/x?

    AP Unit 5AB & BC

    Extreme values & the Mean Value Theorem

    Two guarantees about continuous and differentiable functions: there is always a highest and lowest point, and somewhere the slope equals the average slope.

    The idea

    Extreme Value Theorem: a function continuous on a closed interval [a, b] has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum there. They occur at endpoints or at critical points, where f′ = 0 or f′ does not exist. To find them, evaluate f at the critical points and at both endpoints (the candidates test).

    Mean Value Theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then somewhere inside there is a point c where the tangent line is parallel to the secant line: f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). If you drove 120 miles in 2 hours, at some moment your speedometer read exactly 60.

    Find the parallel tangent
    Function
