    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On x³/3 − x with the default interval, find where the tangent is parallel to the secant.

      What you should see

      There can be more than one c. Each orange tangent is parallel to the secant. The MVT only promises at least one.

    2. On the same curve and interval, read the absolute maximum and minimum. Where are they?

      What you should see

      The maximum is about 2.708 at the right endpoint x = 2.5 (the local maximum at x = −1 is only 2/3). The minimum is −2/3 at the critical point x = 1. This is why the candidates test always checks the endpoints.

    3. Choose x² on [−1, 2]. Find c before you look.

      What you should see

      The average slope is (4 − 1)/3 = 1, and f′(c) = 2c = 1 gives c = 0.5, the midpoint. For any parabola, the MVT point is the midpoint of the interval.

    4. Choose |x|. Does a tangent parallel to the secant exist?

      What you should see

      No: the slope of |x| is only −1 or 1, but the average slope here is 1/3. The MVT does not apply because |x| is not differentiable at 0, which lies inside the interval.

    Worked example

    Verify the MVT for f(x) = x² on [1, 3] and find c.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Check the hypotheses. f is a polynomial: continuous and differentiable everywhere.
    2. Average slope. (f(3) − f(1))/(3 − 1) = (9 − 1)/2 = 4.
    3. Set the derivative equal. f′(c) = 2c = 4.
    4. Solve. c = 2, and 2 lies in (1, 3). ✓
    5. Answer. c = 2. (The tangent at x = 2 has slope 4, parallel to the secant.)

    Worked example 2: speed cameras (AP-style table)

    Highway cameras record a car at the times and mile markers in the table. The speed limit is 70 mph. The car's position p(t) is a differentiable function of t. (a) Must the car have been going faster than the speed limit at some time between 2:00 and 2:24? Justify. (b) Must the car have been going exactly 70 mph at some time between 2:24 and 2:36? (c) Assume p is twice differentiable. Must the car's acceleration have been negative at some time? Explain.

    t (minutes after 2:00 pm)02436
    p(t) (mile marker)124761

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. (a) Average speed. (47 − 12) miles in 24 minutes: 35 miles ÷ 0.4 hour = 87.5 mph.
    2. Apply the MVT. p is differentiable, so it is also continuous, on [0, 24]. So for some c₁ in (0, 24), p′(c₁) = 87.5 mph. Yes: at that moment the car was going exactly 87.5 mph, faster than 70.
    3. (b) From 2:24 to 2:36 the average speed is 14 miles ÷ 0.2 hour = 70 mph. By the MVT on [24, 36], yes: p′(c₂) = 70 mph for some c₂ in (24, 36).
    4. (c) MVT again, on the velocity. v = p′ is differentiable on [c₁, c₂], so for some time between, a = v′ = (70 − 87.5)/(c₂ − c₁). The numerator is negative and c₂ > c₁, so yes: the acceleration was negative at some time.
    5. What the MVT does not tell you. It proves such moments exist, but not when they happened or what the speed was at 2:24. Average-speed cameras in some countries (the United Kingdom and Italy, for example) issue tickets with exactly this argument.

    Common mistakes

    • Using the MVT without checking continuity and differentiability.
    • Giving a c outside (a, b).
    • Finding extremes by only looking where f′ = 0 and forgetting the endpoints.
    • Confusing the MVT (an average slope) with Rolle's theorem (the special case f(a) = f(b), slope 0).
    • Saying a local maximum is the absolute maximum. Compare all candidates.
    • Mixing units: miles per minute is not miles per hour. Convert before comparing with a speed limit.

    The candidates test

    To find absolute extremes of a continuous f on [a, b]: (1) find critical points inside (a, b), (2) evaluate f at each critical point and at a and b, (3) the largest value is the maximum and the smallest is the minimum. It always works on a closed interval; on an open interval an extreme may not exist.

    Check yourself: f is continuous on [0, 4], f(0) = 1 and f(4) = 9, and differentiable on (0, 4). The MVT guarantees a c in (0, 4) with f′(c) =

    AP Unit 5AB & BC

    Increasing, decreasing & the first derivative test

    Where the slope is positive the function climbs, where it is negative the function falls. The turning points are where the sign changes.

    The idea

    If f′(x) > 0 on an interval, f is increasing there; if f′(x) < 0, f is decreasing. A critical point is an x in the domain where f′ = 0 or f′ does not exist. These are the only places a function can turn.

    First derivative test: at a critical point c, look at the sign of f′ on each side. If f′ changes from + to −, f has a local maximum at c. From − to +: a local minimum. If the sign does not change, c is neither (think x³ at 0). Always justify with a sign chart.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    the derivative was a number at a point
    So we didn't need
    its sign tells the whole story of rise and fall
    Now
    finding peaks and valleys
    So we need
    increasing/decreasing and the first derivative test
    f′ > 0 ⇒ increasing · f′ < 0 ⇒ decreasingsign of the slope
    + → − ⇒ local max · − → + ⇒ local minfirst derivative test
    critical point: f′ = 0 or DNEcandidates
    Read the shape from the slope
    Function
    sign of f′ at the point—
    critical points—
    classification—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose x³ and slide through 0. Is x = 0 a max, a min or neither?

      What you should see

      Neither: f′ = 3x² is 0 at x = 0 but positive on both sides, so f keeps increasing. A critical point is a candidate, not a guarantee.

    2. Choose x^(2/3). What happens at x = 0?

      What you should see

      f′ does not exist at 0 (a cusp), so 0 is a critical point. f′ changes from − to +, so it is a local minimum.

    3. Choose x³ − 3x with x = 0. Is f increasing or decreasing there, and how steeply?

      What you should see

      Decreasing, with slope f′(0) = −3. The point sits in the middle of (−1, 1), where f′ = 3x² − 3 is negative, so the tangent slopes down.

    4. Choose x⁴ − 2x². How many critical points are there, and which is the local maximum?

      What you should see

      Three: f′ = 4x(x − 1)(x + 1) is 0 at −1, 0 and 1. The sign chart is − + − +, so x = ±1 are local minima (f = −1) and x = 0 is the local maximum (f = 0).

    5. Choose x·e⁻ˣ and slide x through 1. What is f(1), and why can f′ only change sign there?

      What you should see

      f(1) = 1/e ≈ 0.368, a local maximum. f′ = (1 − x)e⁻ˣ and e⁻ˣ is never 0, so the sign of f′ is the sign of 1 − x: positive before 1, negative after.

    Worked example

    Find the intervals where f(x) = x³ − 3x is increasing or decreasing, and classify its critical points.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Differentiate. f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1).
    2. Critical points. f′ = 0 at x = −1 and x = 1.
    3. Sign chart. x < −1: f′ > 0; −1 < x < 1: f′ < 0; x > 1: f′ > 0.
    4. Conclude. f is increasing on (−∞, −1) and (1, ∞), decreasing on (−1, 1).
    5. Classify. At x = −1 the sign goes + → −: local maximum f(−1) = 2. At x = 1 it goes − → +: local minimum f(1) = −2.

    Common mistakes

    • Calling any point with f′ = 0 an extremum. Check the sign change.
    • Forgetting critical points where f′ does not exist.
    • Not showing a sign chart or a justification (the exam requires one).
    • Mixing up f and f′: the graph of f′ being above the axis means f is increasing, not that f is positive.
    • Reporting x when asked for the extreme value (the y-value), or the reverse.

    Writing the justification

    A complete answer says: "f′(x) changes from positive to negative at x = c, so f has a relative maximum at x = c." Always name the function whose sign you are using, and the interval you checked.

    Check yourself: f′(x) changes from negative to positive at x = 2. Then f has at x = 2 a

    AP Unit 5AB & BC

    Concavity & the second derivative test

    Concavity is the bend of a curve: bending up like a cup, or down like a frown. It is the sign of f″.

    The idea

    If f″ > 0 the slope f′ is increasing: the graph is concave up (holds water). If f″ < 0 the slope is decreasing: concave down. A point of inflection is where the concavity changes, so f″ changes sign (f″ = 0 or DNE there, but that alone is not enough).

    Second derivative test: at a critical point c (f′(c) = 0), if f″(c) > 0 the curve bends up there: local minimum. If f″(c) < 0: local maximum. If f″(c) = 0 the test says nothing: go back to the first derivative test.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    the sign of f′ told rising from falling
    So we didn't need
    the sign of f″ tells how it bends
    Now
    a second way to classify critical points, and inflection points
    So we need
    concavity and the second derivative test
    f″ > 0 ⇒ concave up · f″ < 0 ⇒ concave downbend
    f′(c) = 0, f″(c) > 0 ⇒ local minsecond derivative test
    inflection: f″ changes signconcavity changes
    The bend of a curve
    Function
    f′(x)—
    f″(x)—
    concavity here—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose x³ − 3x and slide through 0. What happens to the tangent line and to f″?

      What you should see

      f″ = 6x changes sign at 0: concave down to the left, concave up to the right. The tangent line crosses from above the curve to below it: an inflection point.

    2. Choose x⁴ and put x at 0. f″(0) = 0. Is there an inflection point?

      What you should see

      No. f″ = 12x² is 0 at x = 0 but positive on both sides, so concavity does not change. f″ = 0 is not enough; the test fails here, yet x = 0 is a minimum.

    3. Choose x⁴ − 2x² with x = 0. Use the second derivative test, then find the inflection points.

      What you should see

      f′(0) = 0 and f″(0) = −4 < 0, so x = 0 is a local maximum. f″ = 12x² − 4 = 0 at x = ±1/√3 ≈ ±0.577, and it changes sign at both, so those are inflection points. Between them the curve is concave down.

    4. Choose x³ − 3x with x = 1. What does the second derivative test say?

      What you should see

      f′(1) = 0 and f″(1) = 6 > 0: concave up at a flat point, so x = 1 is a local minimum, f(1) = −2. The tangent is horizontal and sits under the curve.

    5. Choose sin x with x = 1.5. Is the curve bending up or down, and why does that match the picture?

      What you should see

      f″ = −sin x ≈ −0.997 < 0: concave down. Near the top of the wave (x = π/2 ≈ 1.57) the curve bends down like a frown, and the tangent lies above it.

    Worked example

    For f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x, find the local extrema using the second derivative test, and the inflection point.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. f′. f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), so critical points x = 1 and x = 3.
    2. f″. f″(x) = 6x − 12.
    3. Test. f″(1) = −6 < 0: local maximum f(1) = 4. f″(3) = 6 > 0: local minimum f(3) = 0.
    4. Inflection. f″ = 0 at x = 2, and f″ changes from negative to positive there. The inflection point is (2, 2).

    Common mistakes

    • Saying f″ = 0 means an inflection point. The sign must change.
    • Using f″ to find concavity but writing the answer in terms of f′ (or the reverse).
    • Applying the second derivative test where f″ = 0, and concluding "neither".
    • Confusing concave up with increasing. A curve can be decreasing and concave up.
    • Forgetting that concavity changes can happen where f″ does not exist.

    Two tests, one picture

    At a critical point the first derivative test looks at the sign of f′ on each side; the second derivative test looks at the bend at the point. Use whichever is quicker; if the second derivative test is inconclusive (f″ = 0), fall back on the first.

    Check yourself: f′(3) = 0 and f″(3) = −5. Then f has at x = 3 a

    AP Unit 5AB & BC

    Connecting f, f′ and f″

    The three graphs tell one story. Draw the slope and you can rebuild the shape of the function.

    The idea

    Think of f′ as the slope-meter for f, and f″ as the slope-meter for f′. Where f′ is above the axis, f rises; where f′ crosses from above to below, f has a peak; where f′ has a peak or valley, f has an inflection point; where f′ is rising, f is concave up.

    On the exam you read this information from a given graph (of f, f′ or f″) and justify a conclusion. In the lab you control f′ with draggable points, and f is rebuilt from it. Drag the nodes and watch the extrema and inflections move.

    Assumption upgrade

    Now

    Drag the green points up and down to set f′. The blue curve f is built from it.

    Load an f′

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Drag the middle point of f′ well above the axis. What happens to f?

      What you should see

      f rises steeply where f′ is large and positive, and the bends of f follow the ups and downs of f′.

    2. Make f′ cross the axis downward. What does f do there?

      What you should see

      f has a local maximum where f′ goes from positive to negative. Drag until you see the peak.

    3. Load the “Always rising” f′. Does f have any local extrema? Where is the inflection point?

      What you should see

      No extrema: f′ never crosses the axis, so f only rises. f′ peaks at x = 0, so f″ changes from + to − there: an inflection point where f stops speeding up and starts slowing down.

    4. Load “Touches zero”. f′ reaches 0 at x = 0 without crossing. Is that a max or a min of f?

      What you should see

      Neither: f′ is positive on both sides, so f keeps rising and only flattens for an instant. It is a flat inflection (like x³ at 0), because f′ has a minimum there.

    5. Load “Wave”. Count the local extrema and inflection points of f, and say where each comes from on the f′ graph.

      What you should see

      Three extrema: f′ crosses the axis down at x ≈ −1.75 (max), up at x ≈ 0.25 (min) and down at x ≈ 2.2 (max). Two inflection points, at x = −1 and x = 1, where f′ itself has a valley and a peak.

    Worked example

    The graph of f′ is positive on (−3, 1), negative on (1, 4) and has a minimum at x = 2.5. Describe f.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Increasing/decreasing. f′ > 0 on (−3, 1): f increasing there; f′ < 0 on (1, 4): f decreasing.
    2. Extremum. f′ changes + → − at x = 1, so f has a local maximum at x = 1.
    3. Concavity. f′ is decreasing before its minimum at 2.5 and increasing after, so f″ changes sign at 2.5.
    4. Answer. Local maximum at x = 1, and an inflection point at x = 2.5 (concave down before, concave up after).

    Common mistakes

    • Reading f′ as if it were f. A positive f′ means rising, not "positive height".
    • Looking at where f′ is zero for inflection. Inflection is where f′ has an extremum (f″ changes sign).
    • Forgetting f is only determined up to a vertical shift.
    • Confusing which graph is given: always read the label.
    • Not justifying: say "f′ changes sign from + to − at x = 1".

    Justifications that earn the point

    "f has a relative maximum at x = c because f′ changes from positive to negative at x = c." "f has a point of inflection at x = c because f″ changes sign at x = c." Name the derivative and the sign change.

    AP Unit 5AB & BC

    Optimization

    Biggest area, least material, fastest time: set up a formula for the quantity, find where its derivative is zero, and check it is the best.

    The idea

    An optimization problem has four steps. Draw and name the variables. Write the objective (the thing to maximize or minimize) and a constraint (what is fixed). Use the constraint to write the objective in one variable. Then differentiate, set to zero, solve, and justify that you have a max or min (first or second derivative test, or the candidates test on a closed interval).

    Do not forget the domain: dimensions are positive, and endpoints can be the answer. In the lab the picture and the graph move together: the best value sits at a peak or valley of the graph, where the orange tangent is flat.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    we found extremes of given formulas
    So we didn't need
    how to build the formula from a story
    Now
    fences, boxes, cans, distance and cost
    So we need
    the optimization procedure
    draw · objective · constraint · one variablesetup
    f′(x) = 0critical points
    justify with a testmax or min, and domain
    Find the best x
    Problem

    objective at this x—
    best x and value—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose the fence problem. Slide x to find the largest area.

      What you should see

      The maximum area is 1250 ft² at x = 25 (so the other side is 50). The derivative A′ = 100 − 4x is zero there and changes from + to −.

    2. Choose the open box. What size square cut gives the largest volume?

      What you should see

      x = 2 gives V = 2(12 − 4)² = 128 cm³, the maximum for a 12 cm sheet. Any larger cut leaves too little base; any smaller one makes the box too shallow.

    3. Choose the can and find the radius with the least metal. Compare its height with its width.

      What you should see

      r ≈ 3.84 cm and h ≈ 7.67 cm, so the height equals the diameter. That is true for every volume: setting S′ = 0 gives r³ = V/(2π), and then h = V/(πr²) = 2r.

    4. Back to the fence. Change the fixed amount of fencing to 200 ft and find the best x again. Then try 60 ft.

      What you should see

      The best x is 50 for 200 ft and 15 for 60 ft: always P/4, with the long side P/2. The constraint changes the numbers but not the shape of the answer.

    5. Choose the box and make the sheet 30 cm wide. Where is the best cut now?

      What you should see

      x = 5 = 30/6, giving V = 5·20² = 2000 cm³. For any a × a sheet the best cut is a/6, because V′ = (a − 2x)(a − 6x).

    Worked example

    100 ft of fence encloses a rectangular pen against a straight river (no fence on the river side). Find the dimensions of the largest area.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Variables. Let x = the two sides perpendicular to the river, y = the side parallel. Constraint: 2x + y = 100, so y = 100 − 2x.
    2. Objective. A = x·y = x(100 − 2x) = 100x − 2x², with 0 < x < 50.
    3. Differentiate. A′ = 100 − 4x = 0, so x = 25.
    4. Justify. A″ = −4 < 0, so x = 25 is a maximum.
    5. Answer. x = 25 ft and y = 50 ft, giving the maximum area 1250 ft².

    Worked example 2: designing a soda can

    A soda can is a closed cylinder that must hold 355 cm³ (12 fl oz). (a) What radius and height use the least aluminum? (b) The top and bottom are made of thicker metal and cost twice as much per cm² as the side. What radius and height make the cheapest can?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Variables and constraint. Radius r and height h in cm. The volume is fixed: πr²h = 355, so h = 355/(πr²).
    2. Objective in one variable. Metal = two lids + side: S = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr² + 2πr·355/(πr²) = 2πr² + 710/r, for r > 0.
    3. Differentiate. S′ = 4πr − 710/r² = 0 gives r³ = 710/(4π) = 355/(2π), so r = (355/(2π))1/3 ≈ 3.84 cm.
    4. Justify and finish (a). S″ = 4π + 1420/r³ > 0 for every r > 0, so this is the minimum. h = 355/(π·3.84²) ≈ 7.67 cm: the height equals the diameter.
    5. (b) Lids cost twice as much. Cost (in side-metal units) C = 2·2πr² + 710/r = 4πr² + 710/r. C′ = 8πr − 710/r² = 0 gives r³ = 355/(4π), r ≈ 3.05 cm, and h = 355/(πr²) ≈ 12.2 cm = 4r. Costly lids push the design taller and narrower, which is the shape of the cans you see in stores.

    Common mistakes

    • Not using the constraint to reduce to one variable.
    • Forgetting to check endpoints or the domain.
    • Giving the optimal x when asked for the maximum value (or the reverse).
    • Not justifying that it is a max or min.
    • Mixing units, for example using a formula with radius when the problem gives diameter.

    Common setups

    Perimeter fixed, maximize area: the square wins. Area fixed, minimize perimeter: the square. Volume fixed, minimize surface area of a can: height = diameter. Distance to a curve: minimize the square of the distance (the same minimum, no square root).

    Check yourself: To maximize A = x(100 − 2x), you solve

    AP Unit 6AB & BC

    Accumulation & Riemann sums

    How much water flowed into the tank? Add up the rate over time. When the rate changes, slice the time into short pieces and add rate × time for each.

    The idea

    If water flows at a constant 5 gallons per minute for 10 minutes, the amount is 5 × 10 = 50 gallons: rate × time, which is the area of a rectangle on a graph of rate against time. When the rate changes, slice the time into thin strips, treat the rate as nearly constant on each strip, and add up the rectangle areas. That is a Riemann sum.

    Thinner strips give a better answer. In the limit as the number of strips goes to infinity the sum becomes the definite integral ∫ab f(x) dx: the net accumulation of f from a to b, with area above the axis counted positive and below counted negative. Left, right, midpoint and trapezoid sums choose the height differently.

    Assumption upgrade

    rates multiplied by time only when the rate was constant

    Now
    distance from velocity, volume from flow, total change

    Riemann sums and the idea of the definite integral
    Σ f(xi*) ΔxRiemann sum, Δx = (b − a)/n
    ∫ab f(x) dx = lim Σ f(xi*) Δxdefinite integral
    rate × time = amountunits: (units of f) × (units of x)

    Rate f(x)
    Method

    exact integral—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On x² with left sums and n = 4, is the estimate too big or too small?

      What you should see

      Too small: x² is increasing, so the left edge of each strip is the lowest point and every rectangle sits under the curve. Right sums would overestimate.

    2. Increase n to 60. What happens to the error?

      What you should see

      It shrinks toward 0: the sum approaches the integral as n → ∞. The error of a left or right sum falls roughly in proportion to 1/n.

    3. Switch to the trapezoid rule on x² with n = 4. Over or under?

      What you should see

      Over: 9.28125 against the exact 9. x² is concave up, so each straight top edge lies above the curve.

    4. Choose 4 − x² with the midpoint rule and n = 60. Slide b from 2 up to 3. Why does the total go down?

      What you should see

      Up to b = 2 the total is 16/3 ≈ 5.33, the largest it gets. After x = 2 the rate is negative (pink strips), so the amount decreases, reaching 3 at b = 3. Think of water draining out once the flow reverses.

    5. Choose sin x and slide b all the way to 2π ≈ 6.28. What is the exact integral now?

      What you should see

      0: the gold area above the axis on [0, π] (2) is cancelled by the pink area below it on [π, 2π] (−2). A definite integral is net change, not total area.

    Worked example

    Use a left Riemann sum with n = 3 to estimate ∫03 x² dx.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Strip width. Δx = (3 − 0)/3 = 1.
    2. Left endpoints. x = 0, 1, 2, so f = 0, 1, 4.
    3. Add rate × width. L₃ = (0 + 1 + 4)(1) = 5.
    4. Compare. The exact value is 9, so L₃ is an underestimate (f is increasing).
    5. Answer. 5. Right sum: (1 + 4 + 9)(1) = 14, an overestimate.

    Worked example 2: a car's speedometer (AP-style table)

    A car's speed v(t) is read from its speedometer at the times in the table. (a) Use a left Riemann sum with the four subintervals in the table to estimate ∫030 v(t) dt, and explain its meaning with units. (b) Estimate the same integral with a trapezoidal sum. (c) Is the left sum an overestimate or an underestimate?

    t (seconds)010152530
    v(t) (meters per second)1218211714

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Widths. The readings are not evenly spaced: the strips are 10, 5, 10 and 5 seconds wide. Use each width separately, not one Δx.
    2. (a) Left sum. Use the speed at the start of each strip: 12(10) + 18(5) + 21(10) + 17(5) = 120 + 90 + 210 + 85 = 505.
    3. Meaning. ∫030 v(t) dt is the car's change in position over the 30 seconds. The speed is positive, so the car traveled about 505 meters in those 30 seconds. Units: (m/s) × s = m.
    4. (b) Trapezoids. Average the two ends of each strip: 10(12 + 18)/2 + 5(18 + 21)/2 + 10(21 + 17)/2 + 5(17 + 14)/2 = 150 + 97.5 + 190 + 77.5 = 515 meters.
    5. (c) Over or under? It cannot be determined. A left sum is low where v increases and high where it decreases, and these readings rise then fall. Without knowing v is monotonic on the whole interval, you cannot say.

    Common mistakes

    • Using the wrong number of heights: n strips use n heights, not n + 1 (except in the trapezoid rule's endpoints).
    • Using Δx = b − a instead of (b − a)/n.
    • With a table of uneven times, using one Δx for every strip.
    • Calling a left sum an overestimate for an increasing function. It underestimates.
    • Forgetting that area below the axis counts negative in a definite integral.
    • Dropping units: (liters/minute) × minutes = liters.

    Which sum is high or low?

    For an increasing function, left sums underestimate and right sums overestimate; for a decreasing function it reverses. The trapezoid rule overestimates when f is concave up (the chords lie above the curve) and underestimates when concave down; the midpoint rule does the opposite. Averaging left and right sums gives the trapezoid sum.

    AP Unit 6AB & BC

    The definite integral & the Fundamental Theorem

    Differentiating and integrating are opposites. This theorem is why antiderivatives can find areas.

    The idea

    Define the accumulation function A(x) = ∫ax f(t) dt: the signed area from a up to x. Slide x to the right and the area grows at a rate equal to the height of f at the edge. That is FTC Part 1: A′(x) = f(x). Integration undoes differentiation.

    FTC Part 2 turns that into a method: if F is any antiderivative of f, then ∫ab f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). No more adding rectangles. A related fact: the net change of a quantity equals the integral of its rate, ∫ab f′(x) dx = f(b) − f(a).

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose t² − 2t and slide x to 2. What is happening to A?

      What you should see

      A is at its lowest point (A(2) = −4/3): f is negative until x = 2 (area below the axis counts negative), so A decreases, and f(2) = 0 where A turns around.

    2. Compare f(x) with the slope of A at several x. What do you see?

      What you should see

      They are equal everywhere: the slope of the accumulation graph is the height of f. That is FTC Part 1.

    3. On t² − 2t, move the start a from 0 to 1. What happens to the A graph, and what stays the same?

      What you should see

      The whole A graph moves up by 2/3 (it now crosses 0 at x = 1, because A(1) = 0), but its shape and its slope at every x are unchanged: A′(x) = f(x) whatever the start. Changing a only adds a constant. That is why any antiderivative works in FTC Part 2.

    4. Choose e^(−t²) and slide x to 3. Read A(3). Why is this function special?

      What you should see

      A(3) ≈ 0.8862, almost exactly √π/2 (the rest of the tail beyond 3 adds only about 0.00002). e^(−t²) has no antiderivative made of elementary functions, so A(x) = ∫0x e^(−t²) dt is a genuinely new function, and FTC Part 1 still tells you its derivative: A′(x) = e^(−x²).

    Worked example

    Evaluate ∫13 (2x + 1) dx, and find d/dx ∫0x² sin t dt.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Antiderivative. F(x) = x² + x.
    2. FTC Part 2. F(3) − F(1) = (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 10. The integral is 10.
    3. Second problem: chain rule. The upper limit is g(x) = x², so d/dx ∫0x² sin t dt = sin(x²)·(x²)′.
    4. Answer. 2x sin(x²).

    Worked example 2: a water tank (AP-style)

    Water flows into a tank at the rate E(t) = 6t − t² liters per hour and drains out at a constant 4 liters per hour, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6 hours. At t = 0 the tank holds 50 liters. Let W(t) be the amount of water in the tank at time t. (a) How much water is in the tank at t = 6? (b) Is the amount of water increasing or decreasing at t = 3? At what rate? (c) At what time in [0, 6] is the amount of water least? Justify your answer.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Amount = start + ∫ net rate. The net rate is in minus out, so W(t) = 50 + ∫0t (6s − s² − 4) ds.
    2. (a) ∫06 (6t − t² − 4) dt = [3t² − t³/3 − 4t]06 = 108 − 72 − 24 = 12, so W(6) = 50 + 12 = 62 liters.
    3. (b) By FTC Part 1, W′(t) = E(t) − 4, so W′(3) = 9 − 4 = 5. The amount is increasing at 5 liters per hour.
    4. (c) Critical points. W′(t) = 0 when 6t − t² = 4, that is t² − 6t + 4 = 0, so t = 3 ± √5 ≈ 0.764 and 5.236. W′ < 0 before 0.764, W′ > 0 between, and W′ < 0 after 5.236.
    5. Candidates test. W(0) = 50, W(0.764) ≈ 48.546, W(5.236) ≈ 63.454, W(6) = 62. The least amount is about 48.546 liters, at t = 3 − √5 ≈ 0.764 hours: at first water drains faster than it flows in.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting to subtract: F(b) − F(a), not F(b) + F(a).
    • Adding + C in a definite integral. It cancels, so leave it out.
    • Forgetting the chain rule factor g′(x) when the upper limit is not just x.
    • Treating area below the axis as positive. The integral is net (signed) area.
    • Swapping limits without changing the sign: ∫ba = −∫ab.
    • In amount problems, forgetting the starting amount, or using the inflow rate alone instead of in minus out.

    Properties worth knowing

    ∫aa f = 0; ∫ab f = −∫ba f; ∫ac f = ∫ab f + ∫bc f; constants pull out and sums split. If f is the rate of change of a quantity, ∫ab f is the total change in that quantity from a to b.

    AP Unit 6AB & BC

    Antiderivatives

    An antiderivative undoes a derivative. Because constants vanish when you differentiate, every function has a whole family of antiderivatives.

    The idea

    F is an antiderivative of f if F′ = f. The antiderivative of 2x is x², but so are x² + 5 and x² − 100: they all have slope 2x. The family is written ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, and C is the constant of integration. Graphically, the antiderivatives are the same curve shifted up and down.

    Run your derivative rules backwards. ∫ xn dx = xn+1/(n+1) + C (n ≠ −1), ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C, ∫ ex dx = ex + C, ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C. An initial condition like F(1) = 3 picks out the one curve in the family.

    Now

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Change C. What changes about the curve, and what stays the same?

      What you should see

      The curve slides up or down, but the slope at each x is identical: the slope readout does not change with C. That is why C is arbitrary until an initial condition fixes it.

    2. Choose cos x. The slope of the highlighted curve at x = 0.5 matches what?

      What you should see

      cos(0.5) = 0.878: F = sin x + C has slope cos x, so F is an antiderivative of cos x for every C.

    3. Choose eˣ. What is the slope of the highlighted curve at x = 0.5, and does it depend on C?

      What you should see

      The slope is e^0.5 ≈ 1.6487 for every C, because F = eˣ + C has F′ = eˣ. Changing C only slides the curve.

    4. Choose 3x² − 3 and put x = 1. What is the slope of F there, and what happens to F?

      What you should see

      The slope is f(1) = 3(1) − 3 = 0: F = x³ − 3x + C has a flat tangent at x = 1. Since f goes from negative to positive there, F has a local minimum at x = 1 (and a local maximum at x = −1).

    Worked example

    Find the function F with F′(x) = 6x² − 4x and F(1) = 5.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Antiderivative. F(x) = 2x³ − 2x² + C.
    2. Apply the condition. F(1) = 2 − 2 + C = C = 5.
    3. Answer. F(x) = 2x³ − 2x² + 5.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting + C in an indefinite integral.
    • Using the power rule on 1/x: ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C, not x⁰/0.
    • Differentiating instead of integrating: raise the exponent, then divide by the new exponent.
    • Forgetting to divide by the coefficient inside, for example ∫ cos(3x) dx = sin(3x)/3 + C.
    • Using F(a) = b with the wrong sign when solving for C.

    Check by differentiating

    An antiderivative can always be checked: differentiate your answer; you must get the original integrand back. If it does not match, the integral is wrong. This check catches most mistakes on the exam.

    AP Unit 6AB & BC

    u-substitution

    The chain rule run backwards: when an integral contains a function and its derivative, rename the inside as u and the integral becomes simple.

    The idea

    The chain rule gave d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x))·g′(x). Reverse it: ∫ f′(g(x))·g′(x) dx = f(g(x)) + C. In practice, look for an inside function whose derivative also appears: in ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx the inside is x² and 2x is its derivative. Let u = x², so du = 2x dx, and the integral becomes ∫ cos u du = sin u + C.

    For a definite integral either change back to x at the end, or (better) change the limits: when x goes from a to b, u goes from g(a) to g(b). The areas are equal, which the lab shows.

    2. Choose x/(x²+1). Why u = x² + 1?

    3. Choose x·eˣ² with b = 1. What is the area, and what are the new limits?

    4. Choose 2x cos(x²) and slide b to 1.6. Why is the area smaller than at b = 1?

      What you should see

      The area is sin(b²) = sin 2.56 ≈ 0.549, less than sin 1 ≈ 0.841. Once x² passes π/2 ≈ 1.57 (x ≈ 1.25) the integrand cos(x²) is negative, so the area starts to cancel. The picture in u shows cos u on [0, 2.56].

    Worked example

    Evaluate ∫02 x(x² + 1)³ dx.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Choose u. The inside is x² + 1, whose derivative 2x nearly matches the extra factor x. Let u = x² + 1.
    2. Find du. du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2.
    3. Change the limits. x = 0 → u = 1; x = 2 → u = 5.
    4. Rewrite and integrate. ∫15 u³ (du/2) = (1/2)(u⁴/4) |15 = (1/8)(625 − 1).
    5. Answer. 624/8 = 78.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting to change the limits (or to change back to x at the end).
    • Leaving some x in the integral after substituting. Everything must be in u.
    • Not adjusting for a constant: if du = 2x dx you must replace x dx by du/2.
    • Choosing u that does not make the rest cancel: u should be the inside whose derivative appears.
    • Dropping + C in an indefinite integral.

    Choosing u

    Good candidates: the inside of a power (3x + 1)⁵, the exponent of e, the argument of sin or cos, the denominator of a fraction when its derivative is in the numerator, or the inside of a square root. If a constant factor is missing, it is fine: just divide by it.

    Check yourself: For ∫ x ex² dx, which substitution works?

    AP Unit 7AB & BC

    Slope fields

    A differential equation tells you the slope at every point. A slope field draws those slopes, and the solutions are the curves that follow them.

    The idea

    A differential equation like dy/dx = x − y gives the slope of a solution at every point (x, y) without telling you the solution. A slope field draws a tiny line segment of the right slope at a grid of points. A solution curve is one that is tangent to the segments everywhere it passes, like a leaf drifting on a current.

    Read the field: if the right side depends only on x, segments in each vertical column are parallel; if only on y, segments in each row are parallel; slopes are zero where the right side is zero. Choose a starting point and you can trace the one solution through it. An initial condition like y(0) = 1 picks that curve.

    Now

    Differential equation

    Drag on the graph to move the starting point, or use the sliders.

    slope at the start—
    solution value 1 unit to the right—
    what to notice—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose dy/dx = x. What do the solutions look like, and why are the segments in each column parallel?

      What you should see

      Parabolas y = x²/2 + C. The slope depends only on x, so every point in a vertical column has the same slope.

    2. Choose dy/dx = y and start at y₀ = 1, then at y₀ = −1. What happens?

      What you should see

      Solutions y = Ce^x grow away from the x-axis in both directions: y = 0 is a solution but an unstable one. Segments are parallel along each row (slope depends only on y).

    3. Choose dy/dx = x − y and start at (0, 1). What is the slope there, and where does the solution stand one unit to the right?

      What you should see

      The slope is 0 − 1 = −1, so the curve starts downward. One unit to the right the readout shows about 0.736 (the exact solution y = x − 1 + 2e⁻ˣ gives 2/e). It dips first, then turns up and follows the line y = x − 1.

    4. Choose dy/dx = −x/y and start at (0, 2). Predict the shape.

      What you should see

      The slope at the start is −0/2 = 0, and the curve bends downward as x grows: a circle x² + y² = 4. One unit right the readout shows about 1.732 = √3. The slope is never defined on y = 0, where the circle turns vertical.

    5. Choose the logistic-style equation. Compare y₀ = 1 with y₀ = 3, then try y₀ = −1.

      What you should see

      Starting at 1 or at 3, the solution rises toward the equilibrium y = 4 (one unit right: about 1.419 from y₀ = 1, and about 3.327 from y₀ = 3). Starting at −1 the slope 0.5y(1 − y/4) is negative, so the solution runs away downward from y = 0.

    Worked example

    For dy/dx = x − y with y(0) = 1, find the slope at the start and use the tangent line to estimate y(0.2).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Slope at (0, 1). dy/dx = 0 − 1 = −1.
    2. Tangent line. y ≈ 1 + (−1)(x − 0).
    3. Estimate. y(0.2) ≈ 1 − 0.2 = 0.8.
    4. Check. The exact solution is y = x − 1 + 2e−x, so y(0.2) = 0.8375. The tangent line is slightly low because y″ = 1 − y′ = 2 > 0 at the start: the solution is concave up, so it bends above its tangent.
    5. Answer. About 0.8 (true 0.8375, an underestimate). This is one step of Euler's method, a BC topic: use the new point to find a new slope.

    Common mistakes

    • Reading a slope field as the graph of the solution. The segments show slope only.
    • Mixing up "depends only on x" (parallel in columns) with "depends only on y" (parallel in rows).
    • Forgetting that two different solutions never cross (for a smooth equation).
    • Using the slope formula at the wrong point.
    • Believing the field determines one curve. You need an initial condition.

    Equilibrium solutions

    Where dy/dx = 0 for all x along a horizontal line y = c, that line is a solution (an equilibrium). In dy/dx = y it is y = 0. In the last case of the lab, y = 0 and y = 4 are equilibria, and solutions between them level off at 4.

    Check yourself: In a slope field for dy/dx = y² − 1, the segments along y = 1 are

    AP Unit 7AB & BC

    Separation of variables & exponential models

    For some equations you can move all the y's to one side and all the x's to the other, then integrate. The most important result: when something changes at a rate proportional to itself, it follows an exponential.

    The idea

    Separate: for dy/dx = f(x)·g(y), write dy / g(y) = f(x) dx, integrate both sides, and put the constant C on the x side (once). Then use the initial condition to find C, and solve for y if possible. Skipping the +C before using the starting value is the classic error.

    The model dy/dt = k y says the rate is proportional to the amount. Separating gives y = y₀ ekt. With k > 0 it is exponential growth (population, money at continuous interest); with k < 0 it is decay (radioactive material, with half-life ln 2 / |k|). Newton's law of cooling, dT/dt = −k(T − Ta), is the same thing for the difference T − Ta.

    Assumption upgrade

    Rate proportional to the amount
    Model
    value at time t—
    rate dy/dt there—
    doubling time or half-life—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set k = 0.3 and y₀ = 2. When does the quantity double?

      What you should see

      After ln 2 / 0.3 ≈ 2.31 time units, and again after another 2.31. The doubling time does not depend on the starting value.

    2. Switch to cooling with Tₐ = 1, y₀ = 6 and k = 0.4. What does T approach?

      What you should see

      The room temperature, 1: the difference T − Tₐ decays exponentially, so T levels off at Tₐ.

    3. Set k = −0.5 and y₀ = 8 (decay). Slide t until the value is 4. How long did that take?

      What you should see

      About 1.39 = ln 2 / 0.5, the half-life. Slide on to about 2.77 and it is 2: every half-life halves what is left.

    4. Keep k = 0.3 and t = 3. Change the start value from 0.5 to 5. What happens to the slope dy/dt?

      What you should see

      It goes from about 0.37 to about 3.69, ten times steeper, because the value is ten times bigger (1.23 to 12.3). That is what dy/dt = ky means: the slope is always k times the height.

    5. Cooling with k = 0.4, y₀ = 9 and Tₐ = 1. Compare the slope at t = 0 with the slope at t = 1.7.

      What you should see

      At t = 0 the gap T − Tₐ is 8 and the slope is −0.4(8) = −3.2. By t ≈ 1.7 the gap has about halved (to 4.05), and so has the slope (about −1.62). Hot coffee cools fastest at the start.

    Worked example

    Solve dy/dx = 2xy with y(0) = 3.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Separate. dy/y = 2x dx (valid for y ≠ 0).
    2. Integrate both sides. ln|y| = x² + C.
    3. Solve for y. |y| = eC ex², so y = A ex² with A = ± eC.
    4. Use y(0) = 3. A·e⁰ = 3, so A = 3.
    5. Answer. y = 3ex².

    Worked example 2: a cooling cup of coffee

    Coffee is poured into a room kept at 20 °C. Its temperature T (°C) after t minutes satisfies dT/dt = −k(T − 20) for a constant k > 0, and a thermometer gives the readings in the table. (a) Solve for T(t). (b) Predict the temperature at t = 15. (c) When is the coffee 40 °C? (d) How fast is it cooling at t = 0, and when it is 40 °C?

    t (minutes)05
    T(t) (°C)9070

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. (a) Separate and integrate. dT/(T − 20) = −k dt, so ln|T − 20| = −kt + C and T = 20 + Ae−kt. At t = 0, 90 = 20 + A, so A = 70: T = 20 + 70e−kt.
    2. Find k from the second reading. 70 = 20 + 70e−5k gives e−5k = 5/7, so k = (1/5) ln(7/5) ≈ 0.0673 per minute.
    3. (b) t = 15. e−15k = (5/7)³ = 125/343, so T(15) = 20 + 70(125/343) ≈ 45.5 °C.
    4. (c) 40 °C. 20 + 70e−kt = 40 gives e−kt = 2/7, so t = ln(3.5)/k ≈ 18.6 minutes.
    5. (d) Rates. dT/dt = −k(T − 20). At t = 0: −0.0673(70) ≈ −4.71 °C/min. At 40 °C: −0.0673(20) ≈ −1.35 °C/min. The coffee cools fastest when it is hottest, because the rate is proportional to the gap with the room.

    Common mistakes

    • Not separating completely: all y's (with dy) on one side, all x's (with dx) on the other.
    • Forgetting + C, or adding it on both sides.
    • Using the initial condition before including C.
    • Dividing by something that could be zero without noting the equilibrium solution.
    • Mixing up k signs: k < 0 is decay.
    • In cooling problems, writing T = T₀e−kt: it is the gap T − Tₐ that decays, not T itself.

    Why exponentials

    If the rate of change is proportional to the amount, a bigger amount grows faster, which makes it even bigger: that feedback is the shape of ekt. Check any proposed solution by differentiating: if y = y₀ekt then dy/dt = k·y₀ekt = k y. ✓

    AP Unit 8AB & BC

    Average value & motion with integrals

    The average of a function over an interval is the height of a rectangle with the same area. And for a moving particle, integrals tell you how far it went and how far it ended up.

    The idea

    The average value of f on [a, b] is favg = (1/(b − a)) ∫ab f(x) dx: total accumulation divided by the length of the interval. A continuous function actually equals its average somewhere (the Mean Value Theorem for integrals).

    For a particle with velocity v(t): displacement (net change in position) is ∫ v dt, while total distance traveled is ∫ |v| dt. If v changes sign the two differ. And position is s(T) = s(0) + ∫0T v dt.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On x² over [0, 3], find the average value and where f equals it.

      What you should see

      ∫₀³ x² dx = 9, so the average is 3. x² = 3 at x = √3 ≈ 1.73: the green dot where the curve crosses the average line.

    2. Choose 4x − x² on [0, 4]. Predict the average before you look. How many points equal it?

      What you should see

      ∫₀⁴ (4x − x²) dx = 32 − 64/3 = 32/3, so the average is 8/3 ≈ 2.667, two thirds of the peak height 4. The curve crosses the average twice, at x = 2 ± 2/√3 ≈ 0.845 and 3.155. The theorem promises at least one such point, not exactly one.

    3. Set T = 3 on the motion graph. Compare displacement and distance.

      What you should see

      Displacement is 0 (the signed areas cancel): the particle ends where it started, s(3) = 2 m. But the distance is 4/3 + 4/3 = 8/3 m: it went forward, then back. Distance counts both trips.

    4. Now slide T to 5. Find displacement, distance and position.

      What you should see

      Displacement 20/3 ≈ 6.667 m and distance 28/3 ≈ 9.333 m: the extra 8/3 is the out-and-back trip from t = 0 to 3. Position s(5) = 2 + 20/3 = 26/3 ≈ 8.667 m. After t = 3 the particle only moves forward, so the two grow at the same rate.

    Worked example

    Find the average value of f(x) = x² on [0, 3], and the displacement and distance for v(t) = t² − 4t + 3 on [0, 3].

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Average value. (1/3) ∫03 x² dx = (1/3)(9) = 3.
    2. Displacement. ∫03 (t² − 4t + 3) dt = [t³/3 − 2t² + 3t]03 = 9 − 18 + 9 = 0.
    3. Sign of v. v = (t − 1)(t − 3): positive on [0, 1), negative on (1, 3).
    4. Distance. ∫01 v dt = 4/3, and ∫13 v dt = −4/3. Distance = 4/3 + 4/3 = 8/3.
    5. Answer. Average value 3; displacement 0; total distance 8/3 m.

    Worked example 2: a day's temperature (AP-style)

    The temperature in a town, in degrees Fahrenheit, is modeled by T(t) = 60 − 10 cos(πt/12), where t is hours after midnight. (a) Find the average temperature from 6 am (t = 6) to 6 pm (t = 18). (b) At what times between 6 am and 6 pm does the temperature equal that average? (c) Find the average rate of change of T from t = 6 to t = 12, with units. How is it different from (a)?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. (a) Set up. Average = (1/(18 − 6)) ∫618 T(t) dt.
    2. Integrate. An antiderivative is 60t − (120/π) sin(πt/12). So ∫618 T dt = 60(12) − (120/π)(sin(3π/2) − sin(π/2)) = 720 + 240/π.
    3. Divide by 12. Average = 60 + 20/π ≈ 66.366 °F.
    4. (b) Solve 60 − 10 cos(πt/12) = 60 + 20/π: cos(πt/12) = −2/π, so t ≈ 8.636 and 15.364 (about 8:38 am and 3:22 pm). On a calculator-active question, solving T(t) = 66.366 numerically is enough.
    5. (c) (T(12) − T(6))/(12 − 6) = (70 − 60)/6 ≈ 1.667 °F per hour. This is a rate (degrees per hour, the slope of a secant), while (a) is a temperature (degrees, the height of the equal-area rectangle). Do not mix them up.

    Common mistakes

    • Dividing by the wrong thing: divide by b − a, not by b or by 2.
    • Using ∫ v instead of ∫ |v| for distance.
    • Forgetting the starting position when finding position.
    • Averaging endpoint values (f(a) + f(b))/2 instead of integrating.
    • Not splitting the integral where v changes sign.
    • Confusing the average value of f, (1/(b − a))∫ f, with the average rate of change of f, (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).

    Units

    Average value has the units of f. Displacement and distance have the units of v × t. If f is a rate, ∫ f is a total amount; dividing by the interval length gives the average rate.

    Check yourself: The average value of f(x) = 2x on [1, 3] is

    AP Unit 8AB & BC

    Area between curves

    The region between two curves is made of thin slices. Top minus bottom, added up, gives the area.

    The idea

    Slice the region into vertical strips. Each has width dx and height (top − bottom), so the area is ∫ab (f(x) − g(x)) dx where f ≥ g. Find the limits by solving f(x) = g(x). If the curves cross, split the integral at each crossing so the height is always top minus bottom (never negative).

    Sometimes horizontal slices are easier: width dy and length (right − left), giving ∫cd (xright − xleft) dy. Use them when the region is bounded by curves that are easy to write as x = h(y), or when top/bottom switch.

    A = ∫ (right − left) dyhorizontal slices

    Curves

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose √x and x² and slice with n = 8. How close is the sum to the exact area?

      What you should see

      Close, a little off: the sum is a midpoint estimate. The exact area is 1/3. More slices give a better answer.

    2. Choose y = x³ and y = x. Which is on top, and why must you split the integral?

      What you should see

      On (0, 1) the line y = x is on top; on (−1, 0) the cubic is. The curves cross at x = 0, so top and bottom swap there. Splitting (or using symmetry) keeps every height positive; the area is 1/2, but ∫₋₁¹ (x − x³) dx without splitting gives 0.

    3. Choose y = x and y = x². Slide the highlighted slice across. Where is it tallest?

      What you should see

      At x = 0.5, where the height x − x² reaches 1/4. The area is the sum of all these heights times dx: ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/6.

    4. Choose sin x and cos x with n = 40. What is the area between them from π/4 to 5π/4?

      What you should see

      2√2 ≈ 2.828: ∫ (sin x − cos x) dx = [−cos x − sin x] from π/4 to 5π/4 = √2 − (−√2).

    Worked example

    Find the area enclosed by y = x and y = x².

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Intersections. x = x² ⇒ x = 0 or 1.
    2. Top and bottom. On (0, 1), x ≥ x², so top = x, bottom = x².
    3. Integrate. ∫01 (x − x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]01.
    4. Answer. 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.

    Common mistakes

    • Subtracting in the wrong order, giving a negative area. Use top − bottom.
    • Using the wrong limits: find intersections by setting the functions equal.
    • Not splitting at crossings when top and bottom switch.
    • Integrating x² − x as if it were the area under one curve minus a number.
    • Using dx slices when horizontal slices would avoid splitting.
    • In context, confusing the total area between two rate graphs with the net change (which can cancel).

    Vertical or horizontal?

    Vertical slices (dx): integrand top − bottom as a function of x. Horizontal slices (dy): integrand right − left as a function of y, so you must write each boundary as x = h(y). Choose the one where the boundary does not change formulas partway through.

    Check yourself: The area between y = 4 and y = x² from x = −2 to 2 is

    AP Unit 8AB & BC

    Volumes from cross sections

    Stack thin slices of a known shape along an axis, and add up their volumes. A slice with area A(x) and thickness dx has volume A(x) dx.

    The idea

    A solid is built on a base region in the xy-plane. Cut it by planes perpendicular to the x-axis: each cut is a shape (a square, a semicircle, an equilateral triangle, a rectangle) whose size depends on the base length s(x) = top − bottom. Compute its area A(x), and the volume is V = ∫ab A(x) dx.

    Areas to know, with s the base length: square A = s²; semicircle A = (π/8)s² (the diameter is s); equilateral triangle A = (√3/4)s²; rectangle of height h A = h·s; isosceles right triangle with leg s A = s²/2. The hard part is only getting s(x) right.

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose squares. Where is the slice largest?

      What you should see

      At x = 0.5: s = 0.25 is the longest base, so the square slice is largest there. V = ∫(x − x²)² dx = 1/30.

    2. Switch to semicircles. How does the volume compare with squares?

      π/8 ≈ 0.39 of the square volume (about 0.0131): a semicircle with diameter s covers π/8 of the square of side s.

      (√3/4)(1/30) ≈ 0.0144: every slice is √3/4 ≈ 0.433 of the square on the same base, so the whole volume is too.

    4. Compare the slices at x = 0.1 and x = 0.9.

      What you should see

      Both have s = 0.09: x − x² is symmetric about x = 0.5, so the solid is too. Area A(x) only depends on the base length, not on where the slice sits.

    Worked example

    The base of a solid is the region between y = x² and y = x. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are squares. Find the volume.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Base length. s(x) = x − x² on [0, 1].
    2. Area of a square slice. A(x) = s² = (x − x²)² = x² − 2x³ + x⁴.
    3. Integrate. V = ∫01 (x² − 2x³ + x⁴) dx = 1/3 − 1/2 + 1/5.
    4. Stack them. Every thin square of area A(x) and thickness dx contributes A(x) dx; the integral adds them up.
    5. Answer. 1/30 ≈ 0.0333.

    Worked example 2: the Great Pyramid

    The Great Pyramid of Giza had a square base about 230 m on a side and was about 147 m tall. (a) Using horizontal square cross sections, find its volume. (b) Compare it with a box that has the same base and height. (c) At what height is half of the pyramid's volume below you?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Slice horizontally. At height y (in m), the cross section is a square whose side shrinks in a straight line from 230 at the base to 0 at the top: s(y) = 230(1 − y/147).
    2. Area of a slice. A(y) = s(y)² = 230²(1 − y/147)².
    3. (a) Integrate. V = ∫0147 230²(1 − y/147)² dy. With u = 1 − y/147 (dy = −147 du) this is 230²·147·∫01 u² du = 230²·147/3 = 2,592,100 m³, about 2.6 million cubic meters.
    4. (b) Compare. The box is 230²·147 = 7,776,300 m³, so the pyramid is exactly 1/3 of it. That is where V = (1/3)(base area)(height) for every pyramid and cone comes from.
    5. (c) Half the volume. Above height y sits a smaller pyramid scaled by (1 − y/147), with volume V(1 − y/147)³. Set it to V/2: 1 − y/147 = 2−1/3, so y = 147(1 − 2−1/3) ≈ 30.3 m. Half of all the stone is in the bottom fifth of the height.

    Common mistakes

    • Using the wrong base length: it is top − bottom, not just one function.
    • Squaring after integrating instead of before: A(x) must be squared first.
    • Using the radius instead of the diameter for a semicircle (the diameter is s).
    • Forgetting the constant in the area formula (π/8, √3/4).
    • Mixing dx and dy slices: the slice direction decides which variable you integrate.

    Derivations of the area formulas

    Semicircle with diameter s: radius s/2, area (1/2)π(s/2)² = πs²/8. Equilateral triangle with side s: area (1/2)·s·(√3/2)s = (√3/4)s². Square: s². Keep these in your head: they are the whole difficulty in most cross-section problems.

    AP Unit 8AB & BC

    Volumes of revolution

    Spin a region around an axis and it sweeps out a solid. Each slice is a disc (or a ring, called a washer), and its area is π × radius².

    The idea

    Slice the solid perpendicular to the axis of revolution. A slice through a region that touches the axis is a disc of radius R(x), area πR². If the region has a gap between it and the axis, the slice is a washer: outer radius R, inner radius r, area π(R² − r²). The volume is V = π ∫ab (R(x)² − r(x)²) dx.

    Radii are distances from the axis. If you revolve around y = c, then R = (top − c) and r = (bottom − c). Square the distance, not the function: (f − g)² is not R² − r².

    V = π ∫ (R² − r²) dxwasher, R outer, r inner
    R = distance from the axisaxis y = c: R = f − c
    Spin the region
    Region and axis

    inner radius r—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose the first region. What shape is each slice, and what is its radius at x = 1?

      What you should see

      A disc with radius √1 = 1, area π. V = π∫₀⁴ x dx = 8π ≈ 25.13.

    2. Choose the region between √x and x². What is the slice now?

      What you should see

      A washer: outer radius √x, inner radius x². At x = 0.5 that is R ≈ 0.707 and r = 0.25. V = π∫₀¹ (x − x⁴) dx = 3π/10 ≈ 0.942.

    3. Back to the first region. Move the axis down to y = −1. What happens to each slice?

      What you should see

      Each slice gets a hole of radius 1 (the gap between the axis and the x-axis), and the outer radius grows to √x + 1. V = π(8 + 32/3) = 56π/3 ≈ 58.64.

    4. Now move the axis to y = −2. The region is the same. Why is the volume bigger?

      What you should see

      V = π(8 + 64/3) = 88π/3 ≈ 92.15. The region is farther from the axis, so every point travels around a bigger circle: the washers get wider rings, even though the hole grows too.

    Worked example

    Find the volume when the region under y = √x on [0, 4] is revolved about the x-axis, then about y = −1.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. About the x-axis (discs). R = √x, so V = π ∫04 x dx = π(8) = 8π.
    2. About y = −1 (washers). The axis is 1 unit below the x-axis: R = √x + 1, r = 1 (the x-axis is 1 above the axis).
    3. Set up. V = π ∫04 [(√x + 1)² − 1²] dx = π ∫04 (x + 2√x) dx.
    4. Integrate. π [x²/2 + (4/3)x3/2]04 = π(8 + 32/3).
    5. Answer. About x-axis: 8π. About y = −1: 56π/3.

    Worked example 2: filling a bowl

    The inside of a bowl is the curve y = x²/4 revolved about the y-axis (x and y in cm), and the bowl is 9 cm deep. (a) How much does the bowl hold? (b) How deep is the water when the bowl holds half that much? (c) Water is poured in at 20 cm³/s. How fast is the water level rising when the water is 4 cm deep?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Slice across the axis. The axis is vertical, so slice horizontally. At height y the slice is a disc of radius x, where y = x²/4 gives x² = 4y. Its area is πx² = 4πy.
    2. (a) Add up the discs. Water to depth h has volume V(h) = ∫0h 4πy dy = 2πh². Full: V(9) = 2π(81) = 162π ≈ 508.9 cm³.
    3. (b) Half full. 2πh² = 81π gives h² = 40.5, h = 9/√2 ≈ 6.36 cm. Half the volume sits in the top 29% of the depth, because the bowl is widest there.
    4. (c) Related rate. Differentiate V = 2πh² in t: dV/dt = 4πh·dh/dt. With dV/dt = 20 and h = 4: dh/dt = 20/(16π) ≈ 0.398 cm/s. (4πh is the area of the water's surface: the rise is the inflow spread over the surface.)
    5. Answers. (a) 162π ≈ 508.9 cm³, (b) about 6.36 cm, (c) about 0.398 cm/s, and it slows as the surface widens.

    Common mistakes

    • Squaring the difference of functions: (f − g)² is not f² − g².
    • Forgetting π.
    • Measuring radii from the x-axis when the axis of revolution is a different line.
    • Using a disc when there is a gap (it should be a washer).
    • Mixing up outer and inner radius.
    • Revolving about the y-axis but still slicing in x: slices must be perpendicular to the axis, so integrate in y.

    Which method?

    If the slices perpendicular to the axis are full circles, use discs. If they have a hole, use washers. In AB you slice perpendicular to the axis of revolution (discs and washers); the shell method is not part of the course.

    Check yourself: Revolving the region under y = x on [0, 2] about the x-axis gives volume

    AP Unit 6 · BCBC only

    Integration by parts

    The product rule, run backwards. It trades a hard integral of a product for a (hopefully easier) one.

    The idea

    The product rule says (uv)′ = u′v + uv′. Integrate both sides and rearrange: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. You split the integrand into a part u to differentiate and a part dv to integrate. It pays off when differentiating u makes it simpler (x becomes 1, ln x becomes 1/x) and integrating dv is easy (eˣ, sin x, cos x).

    A good rule of thumb for choosing u is LIATE: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic (powers of x), Trig, Exponential: pick u as the one that comes first. Some integrals need parts twice (x²eˣ), and a few circle back to themselves (eˣ sin x), which you solve algebraically.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    substitution handled products only when one factor was the derivative of the inside
    So we didn't need
    a second tool for products, and for ∫ ln x
    Now
    ∫ x eˣ dx, ∫ x sin x dx, ∫ ln x dx
    So we need
    integration by parts
    ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v duby parts
    LIATEchoose u: Log, Inverse trig, Algebra, Trig, Exp
    ∫ab u dv = [uv]ab − ∫ v dudefinite
    Check the formula against the area
    Integral

    area, found numerically—
    by parts: [uv − ∫v du] from a to b—
    agree?—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose ∫ x eˣ dx. Which choice of u makes the new integral easier: u = x or u = eˣ? Think, then read the formula line.

      What you should see

      u = x: then du = dx and v = eˣ, so ∫ v du = ∫ eˣ dx, trivial. With u = eˣ you would get ∫ (x²/2) eˣ dx, which is harder than the original.

    2. Choose ∫ ln x dx. There is only one function; where is the product?

      What you should see

      Write ln x = ln x · 1: u = ln x, dv = dx. Then du = dx/x, v = x, and ∫ ln x dx = x ln x − ∫ 1 dx = x ln x − x.

    3. Choose ∫ x sin x dx and set b = 1.5. Which choice of u, and what is the area?

      What you should see

      u = x (it becomes 1 when differentiated) and dv = sin x dx. The area is sin b − b cos b = 0.9975 − 0.106 ≈ 0.891.

    4. Choose ∫ x² eˣ dx and set b = 1. Why does it take two rounds of parts, and what is the area?

      What you should see

      Each round lowers the power of x by one: x² → x → 1. The antiderivative is eˣ(x² − 2x + 2), so the area from 0 to 1 is e(1) − 2 = e − 2 ≈ 0.718.

    5. Choose ∫ ln x dx and set b = 2. What is the area from 1 to 2?

      What you should see

      [x ln x − x] from 1 to 2 = (2 ln 2 − 2) − (0 − 1) = 2 ln 2 − 1 ≈ 0.386. The area under ln x is small near x = 1, where ln x is close to 0.

    Worked example

    Evaluate ∫ x ex dx and ∫01 x ex dx.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Choose u and dv (LIATE). u = x (algebraic), dv = eˣ dx.
    2. Differentiate and integrate. du = dx, v = eˣ.
    3. Apply the formula. ∫ x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫ eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C.
    4. Definite integral. [x eˣ − eˣ]01 = (e − e) − (0 − 1) = 1.
    5. Answer. (x − 1)eˣ + C, and the definite integral is 1.

    Common mistakes

    • Choosing u badly (making the new integral harder). Try the other choice.
    • Forgetting to subtract ∫ v du, or its sign.
    • Dropping the product uv in a definite integral: evaluate [uv] at the limits too.
    • Not recognizing ln x needs u = ln x, dv = dx.
    • Forgetting + C in an indefinite integral.

    Twice, or circular

    For ∫ x² eˣ dx, apply parts twice: the power of x drops from 2 to 1 to 0. For ∫ eˣ sin x dx, applying parts twice returns the original integral: I = (…) − I, so I = (…)/2. The tabular method (a column of derivatives of u and a column of integrals of dv) organizes repeated parts.

    AP Unit 6 · BCBC only

    Partial fractions & long division

    A fraction of polynomials can be split into simpler fractions you can integrate with logarithms.

    The idea

    A rational function like (3x + 1)/((x − 1)(x + 2)) is hard to integrate, but it is the sum of two simple fractions, A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 2), each integrating to a logarithm. To find A and B, clear the denominators and match: use convenient x-values (the roots of the denominator), or compare coefficients.

    First check the degrees. If the top has degree ≥ the bottom, do long division first (a polynomial plus a proper fraction). For repeated or irreducible factors the pieces are A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)² and (Cx + D)/(quadratic); the AP course sticks mostly to distinct linear factors. Also useful here: completing the square for ∫ 1/(x² + bx + c) gives an arctangent.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before

    So we didn't need

    Now

    So we need
    partial fraction decomposition
    (px+q)/((x−a)(x−b)) = A/(x−a) + B/(x−b)distinct roots
    A = (pa+q)/(a−b) · B = (pb+q)/(b−a)cover-up
    ∫ A/(x−a) dx = A ln|x−a| + C
    Split a fraction

    A—
    B—
    f(x) at the probe vs A/(x−a) + B/(x−b)—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Use the default values. What do A and B equal, and what is the check?

      What you should see

      (3x + 1)/((x + 1)(x − 2)) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x − 2) with A = (3(−1) + 1)/(−1 − 2) = 2/3 and B = (6 + 1)/(2 + 1) = 7/3. The two sides agree at every probe x.

    2. Change the probe x. Does the equality ever fail?

      What you should see

      No: it is an identity, true for every x except the roots a and b where the original is not defined.

    3. Set a = −1, b = 1, p = 5, q = 1. What are A and B?

      What you should see

      A = (5(−1) + 1)/(−1 − 1) = 2 and B = (5 + 1)/(1 + 1) = 3. Check at x = 3: the fraction is 16/(4·2) = 2, and 2/4 + 3/2 = 2.

    4. Set a = −1, b = 2, p = 0, q = 3. Why is A negative?

      What you should see

      A = 3/(−1 − 2) = −1 and B = 3/(2 + 1) = 1, so 3/((x + 1)(x − 2)) = −1/(x + 1) + 1/(x − 2). The cover-up divides by (a − b), which is negative here. Check at x = 3: 3/4 = −1/4 + 1.

    Worked example

    Find ∫ (3x + 1)/((x + 1)(x − 2)) dx.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Decompose. (3x + 1)/((x + 1)(x − 2)) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x − 2).
    2. Clear denominators. 3x + 1 = A(x − 2) + B(x + 1).
    3. Cover-up. x = 2: 7 = 3B, so B = 7/3. x = −1: −2 = −3A, so A = 2/3.
    4. Integrate each piece. ∫ [ (2/3)/(x + 1) + (7/3)/(x − 2) ] dx.
    5. Answer. (2/3) ln|x + 1| + (7/3) ln|x − 2| + C.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting long division when the top has degree ≥ the bottom.
    • Mixing up A and B when substituting the roots.
    • Dropping the absolute value in ln|x − a|.
    • Using partial fractions on ∫ 1/(x² + 1), which is arctan.
    • Splitting a sum in the denominator: 1/(x + y) ≠ 1/x + 1/y.

    Long division

    If the degree of the numerator is at least the degree of the denominator, divide first. For example (x² + 3x + 5)/(x + 1) = x + 2 + 3/(x + 1), and the integral is x²/2 + 2x + 3 ln|x + 1| + C.

    AP Unit 6 · BCBC only

    Improper integrals

    What if the area stretches out forever, or the function blows up inside the interval? Sometimes the area is still finite.

    The idea

    An integral is improper if one limit is ∞ or the integrand blows up on the interval. Replace the troublesome point by a variable and take a limit: ∫1∞ f dx = limb→∞ ∫1b f dx. If the limit is a number the integral converges to it; if not, it diverges.

    The benchmark: ∫1∞ 1/xp dx converges iff p > 1 (to 1/(p − 1)); and ∫01 1/xp dx converges iff p < 1 (to 1/(1 − p)). So 1/x² has finite area from 1 to ∞, but 1/x does not, narrowly.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    definite integrals had finite limits and a continuous integrand
    So we didn't need
    a limit definition for unbounded cases
    Now
    ∫ e^{−x} dx from 0 to ∞, and the p-test for series
    So we need
    improper integrals
    ∫a∞ f = limb→∞ ∫ab finfinite limit
    ∫1∞ x−p dx converges iff p > 1value 1/(p − 1)
    ∫01 x−p dx converges iff p < 1value 1/(1 − p)
    Area that never stops, or does
    Type
    area so far—
    the limit—
    converges?—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set p = 2 and push the slider out. What does the area approach?

      What you should see

      1: the area from 1 to b is 1 − 1/b → 1. The infinite tail has finite area.

    2. Set p = 1 and push out. Does it level off?

      What you should see

      No: the area is ln b, which grows forever (slowly). ∫ 1/x from 1 to ∞ diverges.

    3. Choose ∫₀¹ 1/xᵖ dx and set p = 0.5. Does it converge near 0?

      What you should see

      Yes, to 1/(1 − p) = 2. A singularity at 0 is tolerable when p < 1: the curve climbs, but slowly enough to keep the area finite. The pattern is the reverse of the one at ∞.

    4. Choose ∫₁^∞ 1/xᵖ dx and set p = 1.5. What does it converge to?

      What you should see

      To 1/(p − 1) = 2. Any p > 1 converges at ∞, and it gets slower to converge as p drops toward 1, where it fails.

    5. Choose ∫₀¹ 1/xᵖ dx and set p = 1. Converge or diverge?

      What you should see

      Diverges: the area from ε to 1 is ln(1/ε), which grows without bound as ε → 0. p = 1 is the borderline for both types of integral.

    Worked example

    Decide whether ∫1∞ 1/x² dx and ∫1∞ 1/x dx converge, and evaluate any that do.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Replace ∞ by b. ∫1b x−2 dx = [−1/x]1b = 1 − 1/b.
    2. Take the limit. limb→∞ (1 − 1/b) = 1. Converges to 1.
    3. The other. ∫1b 1/x dx = ln b, and limb→∞ ln b = ∞.
    4. Answer. The first converges to 1; the second diverges.

    Common mistakes

    • Plugging ∞ in as a number. Always take a limit of an integral with a variable limit.
    • Forgetting the integrand can be unbounded at an interior point, which also makes it improper.
    • Thinking a tail that gets small must have finite area: 1/x → 0 but its area diverges.
    • Reversing the p-conditions for the two types (p > 1 at ∞; p < 1 at 0).
    • Forgetting to split an integral with a problem point inside.

    Comparison

    If 0 ≤ f ≤ g and ∫ g converges, then ∫ f converges; if ∫ f diverges, so does ∫ g. This lets you decide convergence without finding the value, and it returns in the series tests.

    Check yourself: ∫1∞ 1/x3/2 dx

    AP Units 7–8 · BCBC only

    Euler's method

    When you cannot solve a differential equation, you can still follow its slopes in small steps.

    The idea

    Start at the initial point (x₀, y₀). The differential equation gives the slope there. Walk along that tangent line for a short step Δx = h, arrive at a new point, find the new slope, and repeat. The rule is yn+1 = yn + h·F(xn, yn) with xn+1 = xn + h.

    Smaller steps follow the true curve more closely. Euler's method underestimates when the solution is concave up (it follows tangent lines, which lie below), and overestimates when concave down. It is a numerical approximation of a solution you could trace by hand on a slope field.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    a tangent line gave one estimate
    So we didn't need
    a chain of tangent-line steps
    Now
    solving equations that have no closed form
    So we need
    Euler's method
    yn+1 = yn + h·F(xn, yn)Euler step
    xn+1 = xn + hmove right
    smaller h → better estimatebut never exact
    Step along the slopes
    Equation
    Step size h
    Euler estimate at x = 2—
    exact value—
    error—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Use h = 1 on dy/dx = y. Is the estimate too high or too low?

      What you should see

      Too low: the exact y = eˣ is concave up, so each tangent line lies below it. With h = 1 the estimate at x = 2 is 4 versus the exact 7.39.

    2. Now shrink h to 0.05. What happens to the error?

      What you should see

      It shrinks a lot: more, shorter steps hug the curve. The error is roughly proportional to h.

    3. Use h = 1 on dy/dx = −2xy, y(0) = 1. What does the estimate at x = 2 look like?

      What you should see

      It is −1, an impossible value: the exact solution e^(−x²) is always positive. The first step uses slope 0 at x = 0, and the second step overshoots badly. A step size that is too large can give nonsense.

    4. Use h = 0.5 on dy/dx = y. Predict the estimate at x = 2 before you look.

      What you should see

      Each step multiplies y by 1 + h = 1.5, and there are 4 steps: 1.5⁴ = 5.0625 (exact 7.389). With h = 1 it was 2² = 4, and with h = 0.05 it is 1.05⁴⁰ ≈ 7.04.

    Worked example

    Use Euler's method with h = 0.5 to estimate y(1) if dy/dx = x + y and y(0) = 1.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Step 1 from (0, 1). slope = 0 + 1 = 1, so y₁ = 1 + 0.5(1) = 1.5 at x = 0.5.
    2. Step 2 from (0.5, 1.5). slope = 0.5 + 1.5 = 2, so y₂ = 1.5 + 0.5(2) = 2.5 at x = 1.
    3. Answer. y(1) ≈ 2.5. (The exact solution is 2e − 2 ≈ 3.44: Euler underestimates since y is concave up.)

    Common mistakes

    • Using the slope at the old point for the wrong coordinates: use both xn and yn.
    • Forgetting to move x by h each step.
    • Stopping at the wrong number of steps: (xend − x₀)/h steps.
    • Believing Euler is exact. It is only an approximation.
    • Mixing up over- and under-estimates: tangent lines lie below a concave-up curve.

    Why it works

    Near a point the solution is almost its tangent line, whose slope the differential equation gives exactly. Each step makes a small error; many small steps keep the total error small. The smaller the step, the closer you stay to the true curve.

    Check yourself: Euler's method for dy/dx = x + y, y(0) = 2, h = 0.1 gives y₁ =

    AP Units 7–8 · BCBC only

    Logistic models

    Real populations do not grow forever. A logistic model grows fast when small, slows as it approaches a carrying capacity, and levels off.

    The idea

    dP/dt = kP(1 − P/L). When P is small the factor (1 − P/L) is near 1, so growth is almost exponential. As P approaches the carrying capacity L, the factor shrinks to 0 and growth stops. P = 0 and P = L are equilibria; L is stable. The solution is an S-shaped curve with limit L.

    The growth rate dP/dt is a parabola in P: zero at P = 0 and P = L, and largest at P = L/2, where the S-curve has its inflection point and steepest slope. The maximum rate is kL/4. Everything here (limit, max rate, inflection) can be read from the differential equation without solving it.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    exponential growth forever
    So we didn't need
    growth that levels off at a limit
    Now
    populations, spread of disease, adoption of technology
    So we need
    the logistic differential equation
    dP/dt = kP(1 − P/L)logistic
    lim P = Lcarrying capacity
    max growth at P = L/2, rate kL/4inflection of the S-curve
    The S-curve and its rate
    P(t)—
    dP/dt now—
    fastest growth—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set P₀ = 1, L = 8. When is the population growing fastest?

      What you should see

      When P = L/2 = 4 (the steepest part of the S, and the top of the parabola below). The maximum rate is kL/4 = 0.5·8/4 = 1.

    2. Now raise k to 1. What changes, and what does not?

      What you should see

      The fastest rate doubles to kL/4 = 1·8/4 = 2, and the S-curve happens in half the time. But growth is still fastest at P = 4, and the limit is still L = 8: k sets the speed, L sets where it ends.

    3. Start exactly at half the carrying capacity: P₀ = 4, L = 8. Where is the inflection point?

      What you should see

      There is none after t = 0. The population starts at the fastest-growth point, so the rate only falls from there and the curve is concave down the whole time.

    4. Start small: P₀ = 0.2, L = 8, and set t = 2. Compare P with the exponential 0.2ekt.

      What you should see

      The model gives P(2) ≈ 0.521; pure exponential growth would give 0.2e ≈ 0.544. While P is small, (1 − P/L) is close to 1, so logistic growth starts out nearly exponential. Later the two separate completely.

    5. Start P₀ above L (try P₀ = 10, L = 8). What does P do?

      What you should see

      It decreases toward L: (1 − P/L) is negative, so the model pulls the population back down to the carrying capacity.

    Worked example

    dP/dt = 0.02P(1 − P/500), P(0) = 50. Find limt→∞ P, the P at which growth is fastest, and the fastest rate.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Compare with kP(1 − P/L). k = 0.02, L = 500.
    2. Limit. The carrying capacity: lim P = 500 (since 0 < P(0) < L).
    3. Fastest growth. At P = L/2 = 250.
    4. Rate. kL/4 = 0.02(500)/4 = 2.5 per time unit.
    5. Answer. Limit 500; fastest at P = 250 with rate 2.5.

    Worked example 2: stocking a lake (AP-style)

    A lake is stocked with 200 fish. The population P(t), t years later, satisfies dP/dt = 0.4P(1 − P/5000). (a) Find limt→∞ P(t). (b) For what value of P is the population growing fastest, and how fast? (c) Is the graph of P concave up or concave down when P = 1000? Explain. (d) The solution is P(t) = 5000/(1 + 24e−0.4t). When does the population reach 2500?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. (a) Here k = 0.4 and L = 5000. Since 0 < 200 < 5000, lim P = 5000 fish.
    2. (b) dP/dt is largest at P = L/2 = 2500, where dP/dt = 0.4(2500)(1 − 1/2) = 500 fish per year.
    3. (c) Differentiate the equation: d²P/dt² = 0.4(1 − 2P/5000)·dP/dt. At P = 1000, 1 − 2P/5000 = 0.6 > 0 and dP/dt = 0.4(1000)(0.8) = 320 > 0, so d²P/dt² > 0: concave up. Below 2500 fish the growth is speeding up.
    4. (d) 5000/(1 + 24e−0.4t) = 2500 gives 24e−0.4t = 1, so t = ln 24 / 0.4 ≈ 7.945 years. This is the inflection point, the steepest part of the S.
    5. Why fisheries care (beyond the AP exam). If H fish per year are caught, dP/dt = 0.4P(1 − P/5000) − H. The population can hold steady only if H is at most the largest natural growth rate, 500 per year, which happens when the lake holds 2500 fish. This is the idea of a "maximum sustainable yield".

    Common mistakes

    • Using L = the limit of dP/dt. L is the limit of P itself.
    • Reading the maximum growth at P = L instead of L/2.
    • Forgetting the sign: for P > L the population decreases.
    • Confusing logistic with exponential growth.
    • Mixing up P (population) and dP/dt (growth rate) when reading graphs.
    • For concavity, forgetting the chain rule: d²P/dt² needs dP/dt as a factor.

    Solving it

    Separating variables with partial fractions gives P(t) = L/(1 + Ae−kt) with A = (L − P₀)/P₀. You rarely need the formula on the exam: the equation itself tells you the limit, the equilibria and where growth is fastest.

    Check yourself: In dP/dt = 0.1P(1 − P/200), the population is growing fastest when P =

    AP Units 7–8 · BCBC only

    Arc length

    How long is a curve? Approximate it with tiny straight pieces and use the Pythagorean theorem on each.

    The idea

    A tiny piece of the curve over a width dx rises by dy, so its length is √(dx² + dy²) = √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx. Adding them up: L = ∫ab √(1 + (f′(x))²) dx. The polygon with more and more short segments approaches this length.

    The integrand rarely has a nice antiderivative, which is why exam problems are chosen so that 1 + (f′)² is a perfect square, or ask you to evaluate with a calculator. Always differentiate first, then square f′ (not f), and then integrate.
