    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set n = 1 on y = x². How does the one-chord length compare with the arc length?

      What you should see

      A straight chord is always shorter than the curve through the same end points. Chord: √(4 + 16) = 4.47; the curve is 4.65.

    2. Increase n to 40. What happens?

      What you should see

      The polygon length climbs toward the integral from below. The integral is the limit of polygon lengths as the pieces shrink.

    3. Choose y = sin x on [0, π] and set n = 1, then n = 4. What do the lengths do?

      What you should see

      One chord is the base π ≈ 3.142, and four chords give 3.790; the arc length is about 3.820. The polygon always stays below the curve and climbs toward the integral as n grows.

    4. Choose y = (2/3)x^(3/2) and set n = 3. How close is the polygon?

      What you should see

      Polygon 4.647 against the exact 14/3 ≈ 4.667: about 0.4% short with only 3 chords, because this curve is almost straight. The sine curve with 4 chords is about 0.8% short.

    Worked example

    Find the length of y = (2/3)x3/2 from x = 0 to x = 3.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Derivative first. f′(x) = x1/2, so (f′)² = x.
    2. Set up. L = ∫03 √(1 + x) dx.
    3. Integrate. (2/3)(1 + x)3/2 from 0 to 3 = (2/3)(8 − 1).
    4. Answer. 14/3 ≈ 4.667.

    Common mistakes

    • Squaring f instead of f′ in 1 + (f′)².
    • Forgetting the square root or the 1.
    • Leaving the derivative inside √ without squaring: it is (f′)², not f′.
    • Using the area formula by mistake.
    • Not simplifying: look for 1 + (f′)² as a perfect square.

    Parametric arc length

    If x = x(t) and y = y(t), the length is ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt. The speed of a particle is the same square root, so arc length is the integral of speed.

    Check yourself: The arc length of y = f(x) on [a, b] is

    AP Unit 9 · BCBC only

    Parametric equations

    Instead of y as a function of x, let both depend on time t. The curve is the path of a moving point, and slopes come from the chain rule.

    The idea

    A parametric curve is a pair x = x(t), y = y(t). As t increases the point (x, y) traces a path, which can loop, double back and cross itself, none of which a function y = f(x) can do. Eliminating t sometimes gives a familiar curve (a circle, an ellipse), but the parametrization also records the direction and speed of travel.

    The slope comes from the chain rule: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), valid where dx/dt ≠ 0. A horizontal tangent happens where dy/dt = 0 (and dx/dt ≠ 0), a vertical tangent where dx/dt = 0 (and dy/dt ≠ 0). The second derivative is d²y/dx² = (d/dt(dy/dx))/(dx/dt). The arc length is ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt.

    Assumption upgrade

    Now

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On the ellipse, find t where the tangent is horizontal.

      What you should see

      At t = π/2, dy/dt = 2cos t = 0 while dx/dt = −3 sin t ≠ 0: the top of the ellipse, a horizontal tangent.

    2. On the cycloid, put t at 2π. What is happening to the slope?

      What you should see

      Both dx/dt = 1 − cos t and dy/dt = sin t are 0: a cusp, where the wheel point touches down. The slope is not defined there.

    3. On the parabola x = t, y = t² − 2t, put t = 1. What is dy/dx?

      What you should see

      dy/dt = 2t − 2 = 0 and dx/dt = 1, so dy/dx = 0: a horizontal tangent at the vertex (1, −1). For this curve dy/dx = 2t − 2 is just the ordinary derivative of y = x² − 2x.

    4. On the figure eight (x = cos t, y = sin 2t), put t = π/4 ≈ 0.785. What is the slope?

      What you should see

      dy/dt = 2cos(2t) = 0 at t = π/4 while dx/dt = −sin t ≠ 0: a horizontal tangent at the top of the right loop, (0.707, 1).

    5. On the figure eight, put t = 0. Why does the tangent look vertical?

      What you should see

      At t = 0 the point is (1, 0). dx/dt = −sin 0 = 0 and dy/dt = 2cos 0 = 2, so the velocity is straight up: a vertical tangent, and dy/dx is not defined there.

    Worked example

    For x = t² and y = t³ − 3t, find dy/dx and d²y/dx² at t = 2, and the points of horizontal tangent.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Rates. dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 3t² − 3.
    2. Slope. dy/dx = (3t² − 3)/(2t). At t = 2: 9/4.
    3. Second derivative. d/dt(dy/dx) = d/dt[(3/2)t − (3/2)/t] = 3/2 + (3/2)/t². Divide by dx/dt = 2t: at t = 2 that is (3/2 + 3/8)/4 = 15/32.
    4. Horizontal tangents. dy/dt = 0 at t = ±1 (dx/dt = ±2 ≠ 0): the points (1, −2) and (1, 2).
    5. Answer. dy/dx = 9/4, d²y/dx² = 15/32; horizontal tangents at (1, −2) and (1, 2).

    Common mistakes

    • Differentiating dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) with respect to t and forgetting to divide by dx/dt again for the second derivative.
    • Writing dy/dx = dx/dt ÷ dy/dt (upside down).
    • Calling a point with dx/dt = dy/dt = 0 a tangent: check, it may be a cusp.
    • Forgetting that t is time, not the x-coordinate.
    • Using speed formula without the square root.

    Speed and direction

    The velocity vector is ⟨dx/dt, dy/dt⟩ and always points along the tangent in the direction of travel. The speed is its magnitude √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²). The distance traveled is the integral of speed, which is the arc length formula.

    AP Unit 9 · BCBC only

    Vector-valued functions & motion

    A particle moving in the plane has a position vector, a velocity vector and an acceleration vector. Each is the derivative of the one before.

    The idea

    Write the position as r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩. Then the velocity is v(t) = ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩ (tangent to the path) and the acceleration is a(t) = ⟨x″(t), y″(t)⟩. The speed is |v| = √(x′² + y′²), and the distance traveled from t = a to t = b is ∫ |v| dt.

    Integrate component by component to go backwards: position = initial position + ∫ velocity. The particle speeds up when the acceleration has a positive component along the velocity (v · a > 0) and slows down when v · a < 0. Uniform circular motion has constant speed but nonzero acceleration (pointing to the center): the velocity direction keeps changing.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On circle motion, compare the speed at different t. Is it constant? What about acceleration?

      What you should see

      The speed is constant (2), but the acceleration is not zero and points to the center: the particle is always turning. Velocity changes direction even when speed does not.

    2. On the projectile, find when the acceleration changes.

      What you should see

      It never changes: a = ⟨0, −2⟩ at every t (gravity). The vertical velocity decreases, then the particle falls.

    3. On the projectile, set t = 2. Compare v and a here. Is the particle speeding up?

      What you should see

      At the top of the path v = ⟨2, 0⟩ and a = ⟨0, −2⟩, so v · a = 0: the velocity is horizontal and the acceleration vertical. The speed is 2, its smallest value on this path, and it is neither increasing nor decreasing at that instant.

    4. Choose the spiral and set t = 3. Is the particle speeding up or slowing down?

      What you should see

      Speeding up: v · a ≈ 3.0 > 0. The speed is √(1 + t²) = √10 ≈ 3.16 and it keeps growing, even though the path keeps turning. The acceleration has a part along the velocity and a part across it.

    Worked example

    A particle has r(t) = ⟨t², t³ − 3t⟩. Find its velocity, speed and acceleration at t = 2.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Velocity. v(t) = ⟨2t, 3t² − 3⟩, so v(2) = ⟨4, 9⟩.
    2. Speed. |v(2)| = √(16 + 81) = √97 ≈ 9.849.
    3. Acceleration. a(t) = ⟨2, 6t⟩, so a(2) = ⟨2, 12⟩.
    4. Speeding up? v · a = 4(2) + 9(12) = 116 > 0: yes.
    5. Answer. v = ⟨4, 9⟩, speed √97, a = ⟨2, 12⟩; speeding up.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting that speed is a magnitude (square root of the sum of squares).
    • Saying the particle is not accelerating because its speed is constant.
    • Differentiating only x or only y: both components.
    • Using the position vector for velocity.
    • Confusing the path (a curve) with the position function (a point moving on it).

    Components

    Everything works component by component. The x and y motions are independent in a projectile: constant horizontal velocity, constant downward acceleration. For uniform circular motion r(t) = ⟨R cos ωt, R sin ωt⟩, the speed is Rω and the acceleration has size Rω², directed inward.

    AP Unit 9 · BCBC only

    Polar curves & area

    Describe a point by its distance r from the origin and its angle θ. Flowers, spirals and hearts have simple polar equations.

    The idea

    A point has polar coordinates (r, θ) and rectangular coordinates x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. A polar curve r = f(θ) draws a point at distance f(θ) in direction θ as θ sweeps. The cardioid r = 1 + cos θ, the rose r = 2 cos 2θ and the spiral r = θ are all simple in polar form and awkward in rectangular form.

    The area swept out is made of thin sectors (pizza slices): a sector of angle dθ and radius r has area ½r² dθ, so A = ½ ∫αβ r² dθ. The slope is found as for a parametric curve (x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ), giving dy/dx = (r′ sin θ + r cos θ)/(r′ cos θ − r sin θ).

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On the cardioid, sweep θ from 0 to π. What fraction of the total area is swept?

      What you should see

      Half: by symmetry across the x-axis, the upper half of the cardioid is half the area, 3π/4 of 3π/2.

    2. On the rose r = 2 cos 2θ, where is r negative?

      What you should see

      When cos 2θ < 0, for π/4 < θ < 3π/4: the point is plotted in the opposite direction, which draws the other petals.

    3. On the rose, set θ = 6.28 (a full turn). What is the area swept, and what does it cover?

      What you should see

      The total is 2π ≈ 6.283: ½ ∫ 4cos²2θ dθ over 0 to 2π. The four petals each have area π/2, and the sectors for negative r still add area, because r² is never negative.

    4. Choose the limaçon r = 1 + 2 cos θ and set θ = 3.14. What is r, and where is the point?

      What you should see

      r = 1 + 2 cos π = −1, so the point is plotted one unit in the direction opposite to θ = π, that is at (1, 0) on the positive x-axis. This is the tip of the small inner loop, which exists only where r is negative.

    5. Choose the circle r = 2 sin θ and set θ = π/2 (about 1.57). How much area is swept, and when is the circle finished?

      What you should see

      Half of π: the area swept is about 1.57 (π/2), and the circle is complete at θ = π, with total area π. This circle has radius 1, so π is right, and θ only needs to run from 0 to π, not 2π.

    Worked example

    Find the area enclosed by the cardioid r = 1 + cos θ.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Formula. A = ½ ∫02π r² dθ = ½ ∫02π (1 + cos θ)² dθ.
    2. Expand. (1 + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 cos θ + cos²θ = 3/2 + 2 cos θ + (1/2)cos 2θ.
    3. Integrate. ∫02π (3/2 + 2 cos θ + (1/2)cos 2θ) dθ = (3/2)(2π) = 3π (the cosines integrate to 0).
    4. Answer. A = (1/2)(3π) = 3π/2.

    Worked example 2: a microphone's pickup region (AP-style model)

    A cardioid microphone sits at the origin facing the positive x-axis. Model the region in which it picks up a performer clearly by r = 4(1 + cos θ), with r in feet and θ measured from the direction the microphone faces. (a) Find the area of the region. (b) Find how far the pickup reaches directly ahead, directly to the side (θ = π/2) and directly behind. (c) Find the area of the part behind the microphone, π/2 ≤ θ ≤ 3π/2, and what fraction of the whole it is.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. (a) Area = ½ ∫02π [4(1 + cos θ)]² dθ = 16 · ½ ∫02π (1 + cos θ)² dθ = 16 · (3π/2) = 24π ≈ 75.40 ft², using the result of the first example.
    2. (b) r(0) = 4(2) = 8 ft ahead, r(π/2) = 4(1) = 4 ft to the side, and r(π) = 4(0) = 0 ft directly behind.
    3. (c) Rear half. A = ½ ∫π/23π/2 16(1 + cos θ)² dθ = 8 [3θ/2 + 2 sin θ + (1/4) sin 2θ]π/23π/2 = 8(3π/2 − 4) = 12π − 32 ≈ 5.70 ft².
    4. Fraction. 5.70 ÷ 75.40 ≈ 7.6%: only about one thirteenth of the pickup region lies behind the microphone.
    5. Why microphones are built this way (beyond the AP exam). A cardioid pattern rejects sound from behind, which is why such microphones are used on stage next to loudspeakers. Real patterns describe sensitivity rather than a sharp edge, so this region is only a model.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting the ½ in the area formula.
    • Using ∫ r dθ instead of ∫ r² dθ.
    • Using the wrong interval for θ so that the curve is traced twice or only partly.
    • Mixing up (r, θ) and (x, y) in conversions.
    • Treating a negative r as an error: it simply plots the point on the opposite side.

    Finding limits

    To get the right θ limits, find where r = 0 (the curve returns to the origin) for one petal or loop, or use symmetry. Between two curves r₁ and r₂ (r₁ outer): A = ½ ∫ (r₁² − r₂²) dθ.

    AP Unit 10 · BCBC only

    Series, geometric series & the nth-term test

    Can you add infinitely many numbers and get a finite answer? Sometimes yes: it depends on whether the terms shrink fast enough.

    The idea

    An infinite series Σ aₙ is the limit of its partial sums S_N = a₁ + … + a_N. If S_N approaches a number S, the series converges to S; otherwise it diverges. Think of walking toward a wall: half the distance, then half of what remains, and so on. The steps add up to the whole distance: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … = 1.

    The geometric series Σ a rⁿ is the model: it converges exactly when |r| < 1, and then the sum from n = 0 is a/(1 − r) (first term over one minus the ratio). The nth-term test is a quick check for divergence: if aₙ does not go to 0, the series diverges. (The converse is false: 1/n → 0 yet Σ 1/n diverges.)

    Assumption upgrade

    So we didn't need
    infinitely many terms, defined as a limit of partial sums
    Now
    every later topic in Unit 10
    So we need
    series, convergence and the geometric series
    S_N = a₁ + … + a_N · Σ aₙ = lim S_Npartial sums
    Σ a rⁿ = a/(1 − r), |r| < 1geometric series
    aₙ ↛ 0 ⇒ Σ aₙ divergesnth-term test
    Partial sums of a geometric series
    partial sum S_N—
    a/(1 − r), if |r| < 1—
    the series—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set r = 0.5, a = 2. What do the partial sums approach?

      What you should see

      Toward 2/(1 − 0.5) = 4. After 30 terms the sum is within about 10⁻⁸ of it.

    2. Set r = −0.8. What happens, and what about r = 1.2?

      What you should see

      With r = −0.8 the sums zigzag toward a/(1 + 0.8) = 1.11 (converges, |r| < 1). With r = 1.2 the terms grow, so the sums run away: diverges.

    3. Set a = 2 and r = 1. What do the partial sums do?

      What you should see

      They climb in a straight line, SN = 2N, reaching 60 at N = 30. The ratio r = 1 is the boundary: the terms stay at 2, never shrinking to 0, so the series diverges.

    4. Set r = −0.5 and a = 3. Where do the sums settle, and on which sides of the limit do they land?

      What you should see

      They settle at 3/(1 + 0.5) = 2, landing alternately above and below it, because the terms alternate in sign.

    5. Flip the first term to a = −3 with r = 0.5. How does the limit change?

      What you should see

      The limit is −3/(1 − 0.5) = −6: the formula a/(1 − r) scales with a, so flipping the sign of the first term flips the sum, and the sums descend instead of climbing.

    Worked example

    Find 3 + 1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + …, and decide about Σ n/(n + 1).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Identify. First term a = 3, ratio r = 1/3: geometric.
    2. Check |r| < 1. 1/3 is between −1 and 1, so it converges.
    3. Sum. a/(1 − r) = 3/(1 − 1/3) = 3/(2/3) = 9/2.
    4. The other series. aₙ = n/(n + 1) → 1 ≠ 0, so by the nth-term test Σ n/(n + 1) diverges.
    5. Answer. The geometric series converges to 9/2; the second one diverges.

    Common mistakes

    • Using a/(1 − r) when |r| ≥ 1.
    • Starting at the wrong n: a/(1 − r) assumes the first term is a (starting n = 0). For Σ from n = 1 use a₁/(1 − r).
    • Concluding a series converges because aₙ → 0 (the nth-term test can only prove divergence).
    • Confusing the sequence aₙ with the series Σ aₙ.
    • Forgetting that r is the ratio of consecutive terms.

    Repeating decimals

    A repeating decimal is a geometric series: 0.777… = 7/10 + 7/100 + … = (7/10)/(1 − 1/10) = 7/9. And 0.2323… = 23/99.

    AP Unit 10 · BCBC only

    p-series & the integral test

    Compare a sum with an area. If the area under the curve is finite, so is the sum, and vice versa.

    The idea

    The p-series Σ 1/nᵖ converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1. For p = 1 this is the harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + …, which diverges, very slowly: it takes about 12,000 terms to pass 10.

    The reason is the integral test: if f is positive, continuous and decreasing, Σ f(n) and ∫₁^∞ f(x) dx either both converge or both diverge. The terms are the heights of rectangles under (or over) the curve, so the sum is squeezed between ∫₁^{N+1} f and f(1) + ∫₁^N f. The same picture bounds the tail of a convergent series: Σ_{n>N} f(n) ≤ ∫_N^∞ f.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set p = 2 and N = 40. How big can the sum get?

      What you should see

      Never more than 1 + ∫₁^∞ 1/x² = 2 (the sum is actually π²/6 ≈ 1.645). The rectangles are under the curve, so the sum is bounded by the area.

    2. Set p = 1. Does the sum level off?

      What you should see

      No: S_N ≥ ∫₁^{N+1} dx/x = ln(N + 1), which grows without bound. The harmonic series diverges, but slowly.

    3. Set p = 1.5 and N = 40. Compare the partial sum with the bound 1 + 1/(p − 1).

      What you should see

      S40 ≈ 2.298, safely under the bound 1 + 1/0.5 = 3. The true sum is about 2.612, so the 40-term sum is still 0.31 short: a p-series with p near 1 converges slowly.

    4. Set p = 1.1 and N = 40. Does the series converge? How far along is it?

      What you should see

      Yes, p = 1.1 > 1, but S40 is only about 3.68 while the bound is 1 + 1/0.1 = 11. When p is barely above 1 the tail is huge, so the sum is far from finished after 40 terms.

    5. Set p = 0.5 and N = 40. How does SN compare with the integral?

      What you should see

      S40 ≈ 11.27, above the integral 2(√40 − 1) ≈ 10.65, and both keep growing like 2√N without bound. Here the rectangles stay above the curve and the sum diverges.

    Worked example

    Use the integral test to decide Σn=1∞ 1/(n² + 1), and bound the tail after N = 10 terms of Σ 1/n².

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Check the conditions. f(x) = 1/(x² + 1) is positive, continuous and decreasing for x ≥ 1.
    2. Integral. ∫1∞ dx/(x² + 1) = lim [arctan x]1b = π/2 − π/4 = π/4, finite.
    3. Conclude. The series converges.
    4. Tail bound. Σn>10 1/n² ≤ ∫10∞ dx/x² = 1/10.
    5. Answer. Converges; the remainder after 10 terms is at most 0.1.

    Common mistakes

    • Using the integral test without checking positive, continuous, decreasing.
    • Thinking the integral equals the sum. They only share convergence (the sum is a different number).
    • Believing 1/n converges because its terms go to 0.
    • Mixing up p-series (p > 1) with the p-integral near 0 (p < 1).
    • Forgetting the first terms of the sum when estimating: S ≈ S_N + tail.

    Comparing the tests

    The p-series test is the integral test done once and for all for 1/nᵖ. The comparison tests (next module) use p-series as the benchmark: most rational-looking series behave like a p-series.

    Check yourself: Σ 1/n1.5

    AP Unit 10 · BCBC only

    Comparison & ratio tests

    Decide whether a series converges without finding its sum: compare it with one you know, or look at how fast the terms shrink.

    The idea

    Direct comparison: if 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ and Σ bₙ converges, then Σ aₙ converges; if aₙ ≥ bₙ ≥ 0 and Σ bₙ diverges, so does Σ aₙ. Limit comparison: if aₙ/bₙ → L with 0 < L < ∞, both series do the same thing. Pick bₙ by keeping only the dominant terms: (n + 1)/(n³ + 5) behaves like 1/n².

    Ratio test: let L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|. If L < 1 the series converges absolutely; if L > 1 it diverges; if L = 1 the test says nothing. It shines with factorials and exponentials (n!, 2ⁿ) and is useless for p-series (L = 1).

      What you should see

      The ratio is 2/(n + 1), which goes to 0, so L = 0 < 1: converges absolutely. Factorials grow faster than exponentials.

    2. Choose 1/n². What is L, and does the test decide?

      What you should see

      L = 1, so the ratio test is inconclusive. (1/n² converges, 1/n diverges, and both have L = 1.) Use the p-series test instead.

    3. Choose n!/3ⁿ. What happens to the ratio, and what does that mean?

      What you should see

      The ratio is (n + 1)/3, which grows without bound, so L = ∞ > 1 and the series diverges. The terms themselves eventually blow up, so the nth-term test agrees.

    4. In the second lab, choose 1/(n² + 1) vs 1/n². Which test is this, and what does the ratio aₙ/bₙ show?

      What you should see

      Direct comparison: every term is smaller than the term of the convergent p-series 1/n², so it converges. The ratio aₙ/bₙ is close to 1 (0.9989 at n = 30), so limit comparison would agree.

    5. Choose 1/ln n vs 1/n. Why does this one diverge even though both terms go to 0?

      What you should see

      Since ln n < n, each term 1/ln n is larger than 1/n, and Σ 1/n diverges, so the bigger series diverges too. Comparison only proves divergence when your series is the larger one.

    Worked example

    Decide whether Σ n/3ⁿ and Σ (n + 1)/(n³ + 5) converge.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. First series: ratio test. |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = [(n + 1)/3ⁿ⁺¹]·[3ⁿ/n] = (n + 1)/(3n) → 1/3.
    2. Conclude. L = 1/3 < 1, so it converges.
    3. Second series: limit comparison with 1/n². aₙ/bₙ = n²(n + 1)/(n³ + 5) → 1.
    4. Conclude. 0 < 1 < ∞ and Σ 1/n² converges, so it converges.
    5. Answer. Both converge.

    Common mistakes

    • Using the ratio test on a p-series (L = 1 always).
    • Concluding "diverges" when L = 1. The test is inconclusive.
    • Comparing in the wrong direction: a series smaller than a divergent one proves nothing.
    • Applying direct comparison without positive terms.
    • Choosing bₙ that does not capture the dominant behavior.

    Choosing the test

    Factorials or exponentials in aₙ: ratio test. Rational function of n (or roots): limit comparison with a p-series. Terms like 1/(n² + 1) that are slightly smaller than 1/n²: direct comparison. If the terms alternate in sign: the next module.

    Check yourself: lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = 2. Then Σ aₙ

    AP Unit 10 · BCBC only

    Alternating series & error bounds

    Terms that alternate in sign can converge even when the unsigned series does not, and you get a neat built-in error bound.

    The idea

    An alternating series Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ bₙ (with bₙ > 0) converges if the terms decrease (bₙ₊₁ ≤ bₙ) and go to 0. That is the alternating series test. The partial sums swing back and forth, each overshooting the true sum less than before.

    That gives the alternating series error bound: stopping after N terms, the error is at most the first omitted term, |S − S_N| ≤ b_{N+1}, and the true sum lies between S_N and S_{N+1}. Then separate the cases: Σ|aₙ| converges ⇒ absolutely convergent (and so convergent). If Σ aₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges, it is conditionally convergent: the alternating harmonic series 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − … is the classic example.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Set p = 1 (alternating harmonic series), N = 8. Where is the true sum, and how far off is S₈?

      What you should see

      The sum is ln 2 ≈ 0.693. S₈ ≈ 0.635, and the bound is 1/9 ≈ 0.111; the real error is 0.058, within the bound.

    2. Set p = 0.5 and then 2. What changes about the type of convergence?

      What you should see

      For 0 < p ≤ 1 it converges only because of the alternating signs (conditional). For p > 1 even the absolute values converge (absolute convergence).

    3. Set p = 2 and N = 10. How good is S₁₀, and what is the bound?

      What you should see

      S10 ≈ 0.8180 and the bound is b11 = 1/121 ≈ 0.0083. The true sum is π²/12 ≈ 0.8225, so the real error is about 0.0045, within the bound.

    4. Set p = 0.3 and N = 30. Is the error bound useful here?

      What you should see

      The series still converges (conditionally), but b31 = 31−0.3 ≈ 0.357, almost as large as the partial sum 0.386. The bound is correct but nearly useless: terms that shrink slowly need many terms.

    5. Set p = 1 and slide N from 8 to 9. Which side of the sum is SN on for odd N and for even N?

      What you should see

      For odd N the partial sum is above the true sum ln 2 ≈ 0.693 (the last term added was positive), and for even N it is below. The true sum always lies between consecutive partial sums.

    Worked example

    How many terms of Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n² guarantee an error less than 0.01? Is the series absolutely convergent?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Check the test. bₙ = 1/n² is decreasing and → 0, so the series converges.
    2. Error bound. |S − S_N| ≤ b_{N+1} = 1/(N + 1)².
    3. Require less than 0.01. 1/(N + 1)² < 0.01 ⇒ (N + 1)² > 100 ⇒ N + 1 > 10 ⇒ N ≥ 10.
    4. Absolute? Σ 1/n² is a convergent p-series (p = 2), so the series converges absolutely.
    5. Answer. N = 10 terms; absolutely convergent.

    Common mistakes

    • Skipping the decreasing condition in the alternating series test.
    • Using b_N instead of b_{N+1} for the error bound.
    • Thinking every convergent alternating series converges absolutely.
    • Applying the error bound to a non-alternating series.
    • Counting the number of terms off by one: S_N has N terms and the bound is the (N + 1)th term.

    Absolute vs conditional

    Absolute convergence is the strongest kind: rearranging terms cannot change the sum. A conditionally convergent series like 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − … is fragile: its terms can be rearranged to sum to any number (Riemann). In the course, you need to classify a series as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent or divergent.

    Check yourself: Σ (−1)ⁿ/√n

    AP Unit 10 · BCBC only

    Taylor polynomials & Lagrange error

    Approximate any smooth function near a point by a polynomial built from its derivatives. And know how big the error can be.

    The idea

    The Taylor polynomial of degree n centered at a is P_n(x) = Σ_{k=0}^{n} f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)(x − a)ᵏ/k!. It matches f and its first n derivatives at a, so it hugs f near a. Degree 1 is the tangent line; degree 2 adds the bend. When a = 0 it is called a Maclaurin polynomial.

    The Lagrange error bound says how far off P_n can be: |f(x) − P_n(x)| ≤ M|x − a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)!, where M is the maximum of |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| between a and x. Higher degree and a closer x make the bound tiny. This is how a computer can find sin 0.5 or e0.5 using only addition and multiplication: with enough terms of a polynomial.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. On sin x, raise the degree from 1 to 7. What changes?

      What you should see

      The polynomial hugs sin x over a wider and wider interval around 0. At x = 2, P₇(2) ≈ 0.9079 while sin 2 ≈ 0.9093: the error is about 0.0014, and degree 9 cuts it to under 0.0001.

    2. Choose ln(1+x) and move the probe to x = 1.5. What happens as n grows?

      What you should see

      The error does not shrink: ln(1 + x) has a Taylor series only for −1 < x ≤ 1. Outside that interval the polynomials get worse, not better.

    3. Choose eˣ with n = 3 at x = 1. Compare the actual error with the Lagrange bound.

      What you should see

      P₃(1) = 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/6 ≈ 2.6667 against e ≈ 2.7183, an error of about 0.052. The bound uses M = e¹: e/4! ≈ 0.113. The bound is a guarantee, not an estimate, so it is usually bigger than the real error.

    4. Choose cos x and put the probe far out at x = 2.8. Compare degree 2 with degree 10.

      What you should see

      Degree 2 gives −2.92 against cos 2.8 ≈ −0.942, way off. Degree 10 gives about −0.9427, an error near 0.0005. Far from the center you need many more terms.

    Worked example

    Find the degree-3 Maclaurin polynomial of f(x) = ex and use the Lagrange bound to bound the error at x = 0.5.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Derivatives at 0. f⁽ᵏ⁾(0) = 1 for every k.
    2. Polynomial. P₃(x) = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6.
    3. Estimate. P₃(0.5) = 1 + 0.5 + 0.125 + 0.0208 = 1.6458 (true e0.5 = 1.6487).
    4. Bound. f⁗ = eˣ ≤ e0.5 < 1.7 on [0, 0.5]. |error| ≤ 1.7(0.5)⁴/4! = 1.7(0.0625)/24 ≈ 0.0044.
    5. Answer. P₃ = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6; error at 0.5 is at most 0.0044 (actual 0.0029).

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting the k! in the denominators.
    • Using the (n)th derivative instead of the (n + 1)th in the Lagrange bound.
    • Using a polynomial far from its center and trusting it.
    • Mixing up the degree n and the number of terms (n + 1 terms for degree n).
    • Forgetting to evaluate the derivatives at the center a, not at x.

    Reading coefficients

    The coefficient of (x − a)ᵏ is f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)/k!. So if P₃(x) = 2 + 3x − 4x² + 10x³, then f(0) = 2, f′(0) = 3, f″(0) = 2!·(−4) = −8, f‴(0) = 3!·10 = 60.

    Check yourself: The coefficient of x³ in the Maclaurin series of f is

    AP Unit 10 · BCBC only

    Power series: radius & interval of convergence

    A power series is an infinite polynomial. It converges for x near its center, and the radius tells you how near.

    The idea

    A power series centered at c is Σ aₙ(x − c)ⁿ. It is a polynomial with infinitely many terms, so for each x it either converges or diverges. The set of x where it converges is an interval centered at c: the interval of convergence, with radius R (the series converges for |x − c| < R and diverges for |x − c| > R).

    Find R with the ratio test on |aₙ₊₁(x − c)ⁿ⁺¹ / aₙ(x − c)ⁿ| < 1, then test the endpoints x = c ± R separately (the ratio test fails there, so use p-series, alternating, or nth-term). The radius can be 0 (only x = c) or ∞ (all x). Inside the radius, you may differentiate and integrate term by term, and the radius does not change.

    Where does it converge?
    Series

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose Σ xⁿ/n. At x = 1 and x = −1 what happens?

      What you should see

      At x = 1 it is the harmonic series (diverges); at x = −1 it is the alternating harmonic series (converges). So the interval is [−1, 1): the endpoints must be tested separately.

    2. Choose Σ n! xⁿ. For which x does it converge?

      What you should see

      Only at x = 0: the terms n!xⁿ blow up for any x ≠ 0 (R = 0). Compare Σ xⁿ/n!, which converges for every x (R = ∞).

    3. Choose Σ xⁿ/n² and test x = 1 and x = −1. Compare with Σ xⁿ/n.

      What you should see

      Both endpoints converge: at x = 1 it is the p-series Σ 1/n² (p = 2) and at x = −1 it is its alternating version. So the interval is the closed [−1, 1]. Dividing by n instead of n² lost the endpoint x = 1.

    4. Choose Σ xⁿ and put the probe at x = 0.9, then at x = 1.1. What changes?

      What you should see

      At 0.9 the sums settle at 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10; at 1.1 the terms grow and the sums run away. Since this is the geometric series, R = 1 and both endpoints fail (the terms never go to 0).

    5. Choose Σ xⁿ/n! and drag the probe to x = 3. Does it converge?

      What you should see

      Yes, for every x: the ratio is |x|/(n + 1) → 0 for any x, so R = ∞. This is the series for eˣ; at x = 3 it converges to e³ ≈ 20.09, just more slowly than at small x.

    Worked example

    Find the radius and interval of convergence of Σn=1∞ (x − 2)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ).

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Ratio test. |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = |x − 2|·n/(3(n + 1)) → |x − 2|/3.
    2. Converges when |x − 2|/3 < 1, i.e. |x − 2| < 3. So R = 3, center 2, open interval (−1, 5).
    3. Endpoint x = 5. Σ 3ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ) = Σ 1/n: harmonic, diverges.
    4. Endpoint x = −1. Σ (−3)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ) = Σ (−1)ⁿ/n: alternating harmonic, converges.
    5. Answer. R = 3; interval of convergence [−1, 5).

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting to test the endpoints.
    • Stopping at |x − c| < R and writing the interval as closed.
    • Confusing the radius with the interval (R = 3 has length 6).
    • Using the ratio test at the endpoints (it gives L = 1: inconclusive).
    • Forgetting the center: the interval is centered at c, not at 0.

    Term-by-term calculus

    Inside the radius, differentiate and integrate a power series term by term, and the radius stays the same. At the endpoints convergence may change. For example, from 1/(1 − x) = Σ xⁿ (|x| < 1) you get 1/(1 − x)² = Σ n xⁿ⁻¹ and −ln(1 − x) = Σ xⁿ/n.

    Check yourself: Σ xⁿ/n² has interval of convergence

    AP Unit 10 · BCBC only

    Maclaurin series & operations

    A few series to know by heart, and a toolbox for building new ones: substitute, multiply, differentiate, integrate.

    The idea

    The key series (centered at 0): eˣ = Σ xⁿ/n! (all x), sin x = Σ (−1)ⁿ x²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n + 1)! (all x), cos x = Σ (−1)ⁿ x²ⁿ/(2n)! (all x), and 1/(1 − x) = Σ xⁿ (|x| < 1). Everything else can be made from these.

    Substitute: replace x by 2x or x²: e^{−x²} = Σ (−1)ⁿ x²ⁿ/n!. Multiply by x or a power. Differentiate or integrate term by term: integrating 1/(1 + x) gives ln(1 + x) = Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ xⁿ/n; integrating 1/(1 + x²) gives arctan x = Σ (−1)ⁿ x²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n + 1). Series can also evaluate limits and integrals that have no closed form.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Choose e^(−x²). Where does the series come from, and how many terms are needed near x = 1?

      What you should see

      Replace x by −x² in the series for eˣ: 1 − x² + x⁴/2 − x⁶/6 + …. With 4 terms the curve matches well for |x| ≤ 1.3 or so.

    2. Choose arctan x and increase the terms. What happens past |x| = 1?

      What you should see

      The partial sums fly off: the series has radius 1. It was obtained by integrating Σ (−1)ⁿ x²ⁿ = 1/(1 + x²), which only converges for |x| < 1.

    3. Choose sin x. With 3 terms, how close is the curve at x = 2? And with 4?

      What you should see

      With 3 terms (x − x³/6 + x⁵/120) the value at x = 2 is 0.9333 against sin 2 = 0.9093, an error of about 0.024; with 4 terms it is 0.9079, an error of about 0.0014. Each added term widens the window where the polynomial hugs the curve.

    4. Choose ln(1 + x) with 6 terms. Compare x = 0.5 with x = 2.

      What you should see

      Near x = 0.5 the partial sum is excellent, but at x = 2 it gives −5.6 while ln 3 ≈ 1.0986: the partial sums fly off past x = 1. The radius is 1, because it came from integrating 1/(1 + x) = Σ (−x)ⁿ, a geometric series.

    5. Choose sin(x²) and use 2 terms. Where does it follow the curve, and how is this series built?

      What you should see

      Replace x by x² in the sin series: x² − x⁶/6 + …. Two terms follow the curve well for |x| up to about 1 and then drift. No derivatives were computed: substitution gave every coefficient at once.

    Worked example

    Use known series to find the first three nonzero terms of x·sin(x²) and limx→0 (ex − 1 − x)/x².

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Substitute. sin u = u − u³/6 + u⁵/120 − …, with u = x²: sin(x²) = x² − x⁶/6 + x¹⁰/120 − ….
    2. Multiply by x. x sin(x²) = x³ − x⁷/6 + x¹¹/120 − ….
    3. Limit. eˣ − 1 − x = x²/2 + x³/6 + …, so (eˣ − 1 − x)/x² = 1/2 + x/6 + … → 1/2.
    4. Answer. x³ − x⁷/6 + x¹¹/120; the limit is 1/2.

    Common mistakes

    • Not replacing x consistently when substituting (every x in the series changes).
    • Forgetting factorials in ex, sin and cos.
    • Using the sin series for cos (or the reverse): sin has odd powers, cos has even powers.
    • Forgetting the alternating sign (−1)ⁿ.
    • Ignoring the interval of convergence after substituting or integrating.

    Why these are enough

    Differentiating the series for sin x term by term gives the series for cos x, and integrating Σ xⁿ gives −ln(1 − x). The AP exam usually asks for the first few terms, a pattern (general term), or a value computed from a known series, and the error bound.

    Which tool do I use?

    Most of the time lost on the exam goes into choosing a method. Learn the clues, then practice picking.

    The intuition

    Each problem type leaves clues. "Find the slope at a point" means a derivative. "Total change" or "area" means an integral. A 0/0 limit means factor, simplify or use L'Hôpital. "How fast is it changing" with two linked quantities means related rates. Name the method first; the algebra is the easy part.

    Exam format

    AP Calculus AB and BC · May 2027 exam · about 3 hours 10 minutes

    Section I: Multiple choice
    42 questions · 100 min · 50%
    • Part A: 29 questions, 62 min, no calculator
    • Part B: 13 questions, 38 min, graphing calculator required

    Section II: Free response
    6 questions · 90 min · 50%

    • Part B: 4 questions, 60 min, no calculator
    Show your work: answers need the reasoning and units, not just a number.
    How you take it
    Hybrid digital. You answer multiple choice in the Bluebook app. Free-response questions appear in Bluebook, and you handwrite your answers in a paper booklet.
    Calculator
    Only in the calculator parts (Section I Part B and Section II Part A): an approved graphing calculator, or the Desmos calculator built into Bluebook. The other parts are no calculator.
    Reference sheet
    None. You need to know the derivatives, integrals and series yourself; this site's Reference button helps you learn them.
    AB or BC
    Same layout and timing. BC adds Units 9 and 10 (parametric, polar, vector functions and series) and a few more integration topics, and also reports an AB subscore.
    What changed
    For May 2027, multiple choice went from 45 questions in 105 minutes to 42 in 100. Free response and the course content are the same.
